speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I have the pleasure and the honour to present to this House petitions signed by 533 constituents of Glengarry- Prescott-Russell. subsubtopic: OPPOSITION TO PROPOSED CHANGES TO PATENT ACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have the honour to present a petition signed by people of the Province of Manitoba, including residents of the City of Winnipeg, Snow Lake, Thompson, and other communities.
In their petition, they call upon the federal Government not to change the Patent Act relating to prescription drugs. They believe that the proposed changes will increase drug prices to Canadian consumers and unnecessarily restrict the ability of average Canadians to buy necessary prescription drugs.
The petitioners also believe that this attempt to change the law is yet another example of the Canadian Government making concessions to the United States, at the expense of average Canadians, and especially those people whose health needs require the use of prescription drugs on an ongoing basis.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. Brian Mulroney (Prime Minister) moved:
speechtext:
That this House endorses the Meech Lake statement of principles approved by all First Ministers, April 30, 1987 as a basis for Quebec's participation as a full partner in the Canadian Constitution, and as a basis for the establishment, in a spirit of equality and fairness, of a process for considering futher constitutional reforms.-
He said: Mr. Speaker, on May 20, 1980, in a referendum on its political future, Quebec said yes to the rest of Canada. Some seven years later at Meech Lake, the rest of Canada said yes to Quebec.
Hear, hear!

And out of this mutual affirmation of our willingness to live together came a Canadian federation stronger and more united than ever.
That is the essence of the Meech Lake Agreement.
It is about fulfilling the commitment 1 made on August 6, 1984, at Sept-iles on behalf of the Party I am privileged to lead. And it is about a new vision of Canada in which, as I said on that occasion, "The Canadian federation is not a test of strength between the different governments".
It is about a country in which the provinces are active participants in national affairs.
It is about a new federalism in which, "we rebuild the bonds of confidence with the provinces," in a vital federal system that is adaptable to the legitimate aspirations of Canadians in every part of our country. It is about a country in which all regions contribute to a stronger nation. And, Mr. Speaker, it is about a country whose soul teems with inexhaustible resources. And it is about Canadians working together in a spirit of co-operation and harmony to fulfill this country's potential.
It is about our past, and about our future, joined together in a uniquely Canadian wilderness setting-Meech Lake.

One hundred and twenty years ago our forebears established on the northern half of this continent a noble experiment in federalism. Their objectives were clear in the letter of the British North America Act, namely, peace, order, and good government. What a characteristically Canadian statement that is. There is little poetry to it but a strong ring of Canadian common sense.
May 11, 1987
The articles of Confederation served the nation well, but the task of nation building did not end with Confederation. It continued with each succeeding generation; it continues to this very day, for we were born in colonialism, and only over a century and more have we achieved a full measure of sovereignty.
In Sir John A. Macdonald's lifetime the territorial integrity of the nation was assured by the building of the Great Pacific Railway and the settlement of the west.
In the First World War Canada won the right of representation at the international conference at Versaille. The price was a heavy one, paid in blood at places like Vimy Ridge that are inscribed in the history of valour.
In the Second World War the sons and daughters of Canada sailed from the shores of one of our mother countries, Great Britain, to participate in the liberation of the other, France, and then to all Europe. As long as the notion of bravery exists, the contributions of Canadians shall be remembered and honoured.
Hear, hear!

In the settlement and industrialization of our nation, in the epic struggles elsewhere of freedom against tyranny, we emerged as a fully independent state in all but name as our Constitution remained at Westminster. For more than 60 years Canadians sought unsuccessfully to reach unanimous agreement on making our Constitution a truly Canadian document.

Succeeding generations of Canadians have sought a more harmonious accommodation between our two principal language communities. Quebec's First Premier after Confederation, Pierre Chauveau, compared Canada to the double staircase of the Chateau de Chambord's.
"English and French", he said, "we climb by a double flight of stairs toward the destinies reserved for us on this continent, without knowing one another, without meeting each other, without even seeing each other except on the landing of politics."
More recently, Canadians were asking themselves how they could work towards reconciliation, how the legitimate aspirations of Quebec and the other provinces could be fulfilled within our federal framework. That brought us to the referendum of May, 1980, one of the most momentous pages in our history. From 1976 to 1980, we discussed the most fundamental questions of country in the most civilized manner, with the utmost respect for democracy and one another's opinions.
The experience was a difficult one, even painful for many, yet in the end it further awakened us to the blessings of democracy.
May 11, 1987

Soon after that, Canada repatriated her Constitution. And though it was no longer British law, deep down we all knew it would never be truly Canadian until Quebec had agreed to it. For the Constitution is more than a legal instrument; it enshrines a commitment of our hearts and minds to fundamental principles and aspirations. That's why 1 resolved to bring Quebec back into the Canadian constitutional family. For that to happen, there had to be changes, a new way of looking at things.
As I said at Sept-Iles: "If Quebec is weakened, then Canada is weakened. If Quebec is strong, then Canada is strong."

Yet we could not reopen the process, reopen the question, risking the consequences of another failure unless we were assured of some minimal conditions of success.
At Sept lies I set for the Government the objective of convincing the Quebec National Assembly to give its consent to renewed federalism with honour and enthusiasm. I also stated that I would not undertake a constitutional path with ambiguity and improvisation. Once we had established the principles, we had to establish a process, one in which all partners in Confederation could feel that their interests were well served.
All provinces played an indispensable role in this regard. The Government of Quebec, led by Premier Robert Bourassa, drew up a five-point agenda based on its position paper, mahriser I'avenir, which had been submitted to and powerfully endorsed by Quebecers in the 1985 provincial election.
All provinces then agreed at Edmonton last summer that this agenda represented a reasonable basis for discussion, and further agreed with our suggestion that we should settle the Quebec question first.
Ministers and officials worked diligently over the autumn and the winter. In March, I concluded that this stage of the process had gone about as far as it could go without the involvement of First Ministers and, accordingly, I invited them to Meech Lake on April 30.

Our task was to reconcile Quebec's distinct needs with the interests of other provinces, and with the national interest. Any agreement had to be good for Quebec, good for the other provinces, and good for Canada. And it is, Mr. Speaker, the Meech Lake agreement is all of those things. It is consistent with the principles of Canadian federalism.
Hear, hear!

And it opens the door to a future in which Canadians are more united, in which we can address other concerns, such as Senate reform and fisheries, in a second round of constitutional negotiations. From a more unified
The Constitution
Canada, I am convinced we will achieve a more prosperous Canada.
In that spirit, First Ministers came to Meech Lake on April 30. There were just 11 elected representatives in that room, Mr. Speaker, but they represented the interests of all Canadians. Each represented his own province but all, in my judgment, were motivated by the national interest. The more we discussed, the more it became apparent that we could reach an agreement in principle, an agreement that would meet the test of fairness, an agreement that would stand the test of time, an agreement that would open the door to a new federalism based on reconciliation and mutual respect. To their very great credit, the Premiers were determined that this opportunity should not slip away for they knew another like it would not soon present itself again.

With the positive signals Quebecers have sent us in recent years and through the open-mindedness shown by the other provinces, the distinct nature of Quebec society within our Canadian Confederation is now acknowledged.
The dream of millions of Quebecers is becoming a reality.
The accord also clearly recognizes the existence of a francophone Canada centered in but not limited to Quebec, and an anglophone Canada based in the rest of the country, but also present in Quebec. Our linguistic minorities, wherever they live, can therefore count on the solemn commitment of the Parliament of Canada and every provincial legislature.
At the same time, federal-provincial relations will acquire a new degree of flexibility, making it possible to defuse pointless tensions and turn our Constitution into an inspiring, creative force.
In the area of immigration, federal-provincial agreements can be drawn up with provinces that ask for one. Once signed, they will be fully protected by the Constitution. These agreements should address the specific needs of the provinces that sign them, but the federal Government will remain ultimately responsible for setting national standards and objectives.
We have agreed to entrench the Supreme Court in the Constitution, which I believe Members will agree is appropriate, especially given the pre-eminent role of the High Court in interpreting the Charter.
The current legal requirement that three of the nine justices of the Supreme Court come from Quebec will also be entrenched in the Constitution.
Hear, hear!

And a joint procedure for nominating justices will ensure that they are acceptable both to the province involved and the federal Government, which I believe Members will agree conforms with the true spirit of federalism.

May 11, 1987
The Constitution

We agreed that reasonable compensation would be made available to provinces that do not participate in future national shared cost programs, provided they operate a provincial program or initiative compatible with national objectives.
Medicare could very much have been created under this arrangement. The 10 provincial medical programs today vary in a number of respects related to financing of the range of services, but they all meet the national objectives of providing high quality health care to Canadians within a framework of portability, universality and accessibility.
There is every reason to believe that child care can be achieved through the new spending power provision. As Premier Peterson noted in his Canadian Club address last week, this provision in no way inhibits the federal Government from introducing new national programs. The Parliament and the Government of Canada retain the right to act swiftly and strongly in the national interest on behalf of Canadians. That is our responsibility. That is our duty. That is precisely what we have done.
Hear, hear!

Which is not to say, Mr. Speaker, that there will not be discussions and dialogue, but this is very much in keeping with the true spirit of federalism.
We reinforced the equality of the provinces by placing all national institutions under the unanimity rule. Unanimity was achieved on unemployment insurance in 1940, old age pensions in 1951, supplementary benefits in 1964 and the Meech Lake Agreement in 1987. So it is difficult, very difficult, to sustain the thesis that unanimity would be a straightjacket.
Consider what the absence of unanimity-the absence of Quebec from the constitutional accord, for example-would mean for Canada if allowed to extend over years and then decades. Consider what the absence of Quebec from the Canadian confederation over decades would mean. Consider the corrosive and debilitating implications of that as one weighs the value of the strengthened unity that comes from the Meech Lake Accord.
As Eugene Forsey, a firm advocate of a strong federal Government and a noted constitutional authority has stated:
If we want to get results and get Quebec and the other provinces alike
satisfied, we have to pay a certain price. And, on the whole, it looks to me that
the price that would be paid is not an unreasonable one.
There will be an annual First Ministers' Conference on the economy and other questions that arise in the management of a federation, a proposal already introduced and acted upon by this Government. There will be an annual First Ministers' Conference on the Constitution which will pursue Senate reform, roles and responsibilities in the fishery and other important questions.
Until Senate reform is achieved, there will be a joint federal-provincial procedure for new appointments. This should be
taken as a sign of good faith on our part. Make no mistake about it, we are intent on Senate reform, Mr. Speaker. As I indicated in Alberta last week, we will be placing a specific proposal for Senate reform on the table at the First Ministers' Conference next year.
Hear, hear!

There remains the important unfinished business of achieving a constitutional amendment on aboriginal self-government. Four First Minister's Conferences have been held in this matter. I have participated actively in two. I understand the challenge and the importance. I know this Parliament has contributed mightily in trying to achieve that vital accord that will bring justice to our native peoples. Regrettably, a consensus has eluded Canadians each time. I say to the aboriginal leadership and to the provinces, the Government of Canada remains prepared to work with you toward this objective, but, as with the Quebec issue, the conditions must be conducive to success for we dare not risk failure another time.
Officials have been working on a draft to be approved by the premiers at our next meeting. I have invited the Premiers to meet here during the first week of June. Assuming a formal agreement is reached, we will then table the appropriate resolution in Parliament at the earliest subsequent opportunity. I would hope that the provinces would do the same. Members of the House of Commons will then have ample opportunity to join in the debate on the resolution.
The Meech Lake Agreement represents a conscious act of nation building by all First Ministers, requiring generosity of spirit and a deep understanding on all sides. By recognizing the distinctiveness Quebec brings to Canada, we affirm our identity as a nation and strengthen our sovereignty as a people.
Hear, hear!

By adopting new constitutional and institutional arrangements, we will also provide an opportunity for more harmonious relations between the federal and the provincial Governments.

By civilizing the use of the spending power, clarifying roles and responsibilities in immigration, which is an area of joint jurisdiction, and constitutionalizing First Ministers' Conferences, we create opportunities for concerted government action from which all Canadians will benefit.
Joint procedures for Supreme Court and Senate appointments will reinforce the legitimacy of federal institutions.

I have been heartened by the response of ordinary Canadians to the Meech Lake Accord. People on the street, school children, farmers in the fields of Saskatchewan, strongly
May 11, 1987

support this statement of national unity. That is what this is all about, nation building.
I pay tribute to the First Ministers whose leadership and resolve have strengthened our federation and enriched our citizenship. From every region of Canada, from all political Parties, the First Ministers came to Meech Lake and theirs were the voices of confidence and unity and of belief in the greatness of Canada.
Hear, hear!

Let no one say our national unity is undermined by respecting differences and incorporating them in a common entity in the custody of a central authority.
It would be astounding if the nation that succeeded in resisting disunity felt more threatened by unity.
Together we ventured out on a long and difficult road in search of our political indentity and constitutional sovereignty. Yet we never lost faith in ourselves, we never denied our tradition of tolerance and we never doubted that, somewhere at the end of our quest for democratic dialogue, a fraternal and honourable solution awaited us.
Success is now within our grasp.
I appeal to the civic spirit of every Member of this House so that we may put aside Party politics at this great moment in our history, this hour of strength drawn from our rediscovered solidarity.
Hear, hear!

This is what our fellow-citizens expect from us, from one end of this country to another in a great spirit of hope. We will do honour to ourselves not to disappoint them.

From Macdonald to Laurier, from King to Diefenbaker, from Meighen to Pearson, from Bennett to St. Laurent to Trudeau, the overriding objective of all Canadian Prime Ministers has been a strong and a united Canada. The Meech Lake Agreement contributes to that unity and is a statement as well of a vision of Canada, a vision that is rooted in our love of this country, our pride in its people, our respect for its traditions, our joy at its promise. But that promise shall be realized only in unity, only in the unity that comes from English and French Canadians, east and west, new Canadians and old, together, finally together in a strong and united Canada.
Hear, hear!

speakeroldname: Right Hon. John N. Turner (Leader of the Opposition):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we are embarking today upon what is one of the most important discussions or debates any nation can face, the revision of our Constitution. Canadians are familiar with constitutional discussions and with constitutional differences. We have been talking about it in earnest for at least two
The Constitution
decades and this is why I welcome the opportunity to restate my views once again this morning.
When the Constitution was patriated in 1982, the agreement contained one tragic flaw. In our attempt to break away from our colonial past, one of our most important and founding provinces was missing in that agreement, Quebec.

Since patriation, Quebec's absence has been deeply felt by all parties, and we have focused all our efforts on finding the fairest and most equitable way to complete this unfinished task.
I am proud to lead a Party that has always been in the forefront of constitutional thinking and debate.
Last year, I was the first to present a set of recommendations for enabling Quebecers to sign the Canadian Constitution with pride and dignity. These proposals were enthusiastically received by the Government of Quebec.
We were thus able to raise this debate above partisan considerations and to create a genuine climate of mutual understanding and generosity, the impact of which has surely contributed to the success of the meeting at Meech Lake.

I would like at this time to recognize and pay tribute to my caucus and my Party for pursuing this issue with vigour and commitment. Following the election of the Bourassa Government in Quebec, there was a new spirit of co-operation and a political will to participate fully in our confederation. I'am very pleased that that spirit has been given some substance in the agreement we are discussing today. I know from my own participation in the Victoria conference in 1971 that the process of constitutional reform is long and difficult.
I also must pause and congratulate all the First Ministers on reaching an agreement on a process which may in fact see Quebec brought into the constitutional agreement.
[ Translation]
The question of Quebec's place in the Canadian federation lies at the very the heart of our existence as a nation. The political history buffs among us are aware that ever since the end of the 18th century, attempts have been made to provide for a political structure that would allow Quebecers then referred to as "Canadiens", to protect their rights and safeguard their identity.
The beginnings of parliamentary democracy in our country were difficult, both in Upper and Lower Canada. The 1837 rebellions and the morass in which the Government of Union found itself led the British authorities to conclude that it was utopian to consider imposing or forcing on Canada a uniform system of government.
Clearly, what was needed was a political framework that would leave room for developing views and maintaining

May 11, 1987
The Constitution
identities, while involving all participants in the building and development of a great nation.
Despite the hope that the fears of the past would prove to be unfounded, subsequent events soon showed Quebecers that when the majority spoke, Quebec's appeals could meet a wall of indifference. The Riel affair, the Manitoba schools question, Regulation 17 in Ontario, conscription during the two World Wars and the battles for provincial autonomy are some of the events in this century that were instrumental in convincing Lester B. Pearson, as Prime Minister of Canada, to set up the Commission on Bilingualism and Biculturalism. The Lauren-deau-Dunton Commission sent out a clear and unmistakable signal: the country would fall apart if there was no thorough reform.
Many of these tensions were of course centred in Quebec, but they existed elsewhere in Canada since the very beginning: regional tensions, mostly in the west but also in the north and the Maritimes, which often complained they were not equal partners.

The Government of Pierre Elliott Trudeau heard the alarm signal. In Victoria in 1971 we tabled a proposal which remains a model and inspiration for anyone looking for a definition of a political consensus in this country.

Mr. Speaker, I had the privilege of being Minister of Justice at the time. The feeling was one of euphoria. The Official Languages Act had just been passed by the Parliament of Canada. The 10 provinces had given their agreement in principle to a formula that recognized the linguistic duality of this country: bilingualism in Quebec, Ontario, New Brunswick and even Newfoundland. The amending formula gave veto rights to Quebec and to each of this country's regions.
Despite this very considerable progress, the Government of Quebec finally withdrew its agreement under increasing pressure from public opinion in that province. It was clear that feelings were running so high they could no longer be ignored.
The Parti Quebecois rode the waves which were to carry Quebec to its own destiny after severing its links with the rest of the country. Indeed, concerted efforts were made throughout this decade to revamp our institutions and adjust Canada's orientations to the heartfelt aspirations of Quebecers. But the referendum process had already been launched and nothing would be possible until such time as Quebecers would be given an opportunity to have their say about their Canadian partnership.
The majority of Quebecers said yes to Canada, and it is because they sent this signal that the reform process began through the Constitution Act of 1982. The statement of principles which is now on the table of the House raises the fundamental question about the kind of country, the kind of Canada in which we want to live. The question is two-fold.
What guarantees of cultural security are offered to Quebec? What is the role of the Canadian and provincial Governments with respect to the linguistic duality of our country?
In other words, what common values do Canadians share, what institutions will interpret them?
Some people believe that Quebec must be a province like the others, for any concession on anything whatsoever opens the door to separatism. They see Canada as a solid block, unable to reflect various aspirations yet party to the same principles of freedom and democracy.
Quebec seeks certain guarantees concerning its distinctive character, its population growth, its presence within federal institutions, its freedom to use as it sees fit its legislative powers as described in the Act of 1867 and, especially, its participation in the Canadian whole.

Quebecers do not want to lock themselves into a ghetto. History has demonstrated that they are an essential part of the Canadian identity. They represent a unique fact in Canadian life.

History indicates as well that Canada cannot exist without Quebec and that Quebecers must be an integral part of the life and institutions of Canada.
Nor is the Canadian Government's role restricted to that of a passive observer, for it rightfully assumes responsibility for ensuring the presence and expansion of the French fact throughout the country and elsewhere in the world.
It must constantly define this responsibility and adjust it to new conditions and more exacting challenges. Such is the major outline of today's debate on the agreement in principle hammered out at Meech Lake.
Mr. Speaker, the motion under consideration today is premature because we have yet to see the final legal text of the Meech Lake agreement. Even so we take a positive and constructive approach towards any constitutional proposition aimed at making Quebecers full-fledged partners in the Confederation of Canada. Mr. Speaker, this is why we endorse this motion.

1 believe that the motion before us, Your Honour, is somewhat premature since we have yet to see any final wording or precise text. However, we in this Party intend to respond constructively and positively to any constitutional proposal which will make Quebec a full partner in our Confederation.
Hear, hear!

That is why we support this motion. However, in doing so, I want to make it perfectly
May 11, 1987

clear that we do not interpret this motion as a blind endorsement of the statement of principles agreed upon at Meech Lake. We have serious concerns about some aspects of that statement and will certainly have suggestions for improvements, now and when we see the final text.
We view this motion as seeking our agreement to continue, as the motion puts it, a process to bring Quebec into the Constitution. We certainly do and will support any efforts to that effect. It is indeed a good day for Canada and for Quebec. I have always believed that it was essential to the future of this country that Quebec be a major and leading partner in our Confederation and a full-fledged participant in its evolution. I personally support the motion because Quebec's participation will be necessary for any future evolution of the country.
I believe that the constructive work done by my Party contributed substantially to creating the favourable atmosphere in Quebec and throughout the country for this discussion. We have steadfastly refrained from politicizing this question in the House of Commons or across Canada. We have purposely avoided embarrassing the Government on this issue during the course of the negotiations. We knew that the provincial Premiers and the representatives of the Government of Canada were studying the views set forth by Quebec and that the interests of the country take precedence over any partisan views.
The key words in this motion, Mr. Speaker, are that this House accept the statement of principles tabled by the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) last week "as a basis" for further discussion. In the absence of anything else, we believe that the statement of principles is as good a place to start as any.
At the same time, I view this as a general framework for discussion, not the final solution. As Premier Pawley stated, we must all ensure that the legal wording does not distort either the intentions of the Meech Lake Accord, or indeed the intentions of the Constitution itself.
I also want to emphasize that we will insist upon full committee hearings of the final text which will be produced by the Government of Canada, and a full debate in this House when we see the final results, preferably before the issue goes to the Premiers. Parliament has a right to see this text in final form before it is again negotiated with the Premiers. This is too important an issue for a one-day debate. This is the Constitution of Canada.
Hear, hear!

Of course Hon. Members recall that in 1981 the Trudeau Goverment tabled in this House the final text of the constitutional resolution and this was the topic of a debate. But before receiving the approval of the House the text was analyzed, scrutinized and, let us admit it, improved as a result of the work of a joint committee of the House and of the Senate which sat to give it exceptionally serious consideration over a number of weeks. Mr. Speaker, I
The Constitution
believe that if the House sees fit to strike a parliamentary committee to review, analyze and improve all its legislation, surely we ought to take as serious an approach towards amendments to the basic law of the land, the Constitution.

To do less in this case would be to abdicate our responsibilities as legislators. It is critical that what we do for ordinary Bills in this House, that it, clause by clause review in committee, we should certainly do for the most fundamental law in our country, the Constitution of Canada.
We as legislators must be as precise as possible in our language. We must give the courts clear guidance and an indication as to how we want our Constitution interpreted, what principles we want them to adhere to when adjudicating individual cases. We do not want the Supreme Court of Canada to act as a legislator. That is our role. That is why I believe we need clear and precise language in our Constitution. That is why I believe Parliament has a right and a duty to inspect that language at an early opportunity. We must ensure that, as far as is humanly possible, we look at each provision and try to predict the consequences of them.
On balance, what we see in this statement is positive both for Canada and for Quebec. However, it can remain positive only if its spirit and intent are accurately translated into legal terms.
I believe that the purpose of this debate today-which we welcome-will be to provide to the drafters our advice and guidance on what should or should not be in the final resolution. Our Constitution is the foundation on which our federation spells out how certain powers and obligations are shared, which are exclusive to either level of jurisdiction and, in the case of the Charter, which powers are beyond the reach of either level of Government. Constitutional change is not something which should be done in haste, in a single day before the national forum. It is not something which should be entered into without taking full account of all the implications.
With the provision to constitutionalize two yearly meetings of First Ministers, one on the Constitution and one on the economy, are we not creating yet another level of government, one that meets behind closed doors away from the public eye to change the course of Canada without the prior authority, approval, or even inspection of Parliament?
Will this mean, for example, that we will have abandoned a regional role for the Senate, a body which we believe should be elected? We believe an elected Senate could serve the role of representing the regions on an ongoing basis in an open and public manner. We must be fully aware of the choice we are making and what that choice means to the future of our country. Our role, Mr. Speaker, in this House, in the absence of the precise language which the First Ministers may have in mind, is to look at each statement of principle and try to interpret the impact of these statements and to make improvements where possible.

May 11, 1987
The Constitution
We are talking about a process. We are asking the Government to give us the thinking behind some of these provisions. We need greater detail than we have heard so far. What are some of the ramifications of these provisions? Let us begin at the beginning of the statement of principles.

First, the distinct society. Mr. Speaker, since our convention last November, more than 90 per cent of the Liberal delegates have acknowledged the distinct character of Quebec, with its language, its culture, its specific features such as the use of the Civil Code, and even to a certain extent, its humour, its way of life, is different from other Canadian provinces. We think that is one aspect of the rich heritage left to us by the founding fathers of our great country.
We described, with some inspiration 1 believe, Quebec as the major, but not exclusive, source of the French language and culture in Canada, for it is the major source of energy, of cultural and linguistic inspiration for our French speaking community.
However, Mr. Speaker, we have also taken great care to recognize in our resolution all the distinctive features of our diversified society, including first the linguistic duality of our country which we hope will not only be maintained, but also reinforced in every region of Canada.
We should add to that-and 1 am disappointed that the Meech Lake draft agreement does not-the multicultural character of our society, and in particular the respect of the various origins and cultures as well as the various regional specificities which all combine to make the Canadian society.
We also suggested that the contribution of native people in Canada should be included in the opening section of our constitution, and 1 can only regret the fact that native people were ignored in the Meech Lake statement drafted by the Premiers and the Prime Minister.
We therefore want, Mr. Speaker, to repeat that we recognize the distinct character of Quebec, as well as of all the dynamic entities of our society.
Our Party has overwhelmingly endorsed the concept of a distinct character for Quebec recognized in our Constitution and we will continue to support that concept. In our November resolution we outlined our firm belief that Quebec is the principal but not the exclusive source of French language and culture in Canada. However, we took great care in recognizing not only the linguistic duality of our country, but also the multicultural nature of our society and the contribution of our aboriginal peoples. We believe this Accord could be greatly improved with the inclusion of both these elements.
We also need to know more precisely what the two phrases "distinct identity" and "distinct society" mean. Our proposal in November was that this reference would appear in the
preamble to the Constitution. However, Senator Lowell Murray has stated that those phrases will appear in the body of the Constitution. In my view, that has the potential to change the interpretation of that particular section a great deal. We look forward to hearing the Government's interpretation of that situation.
Already, the Government of Quebec has stated that it will examine the possibility of proposing that the phrasing be strengthened. Others have suggested that it can lead to a constitutional interpretation that language rights of francophone minorities outside Quebec may not be sufficiently protected. It is for these reasons that we believe the language must be clear and precise.
Let me turn to immigration. Again, in our November proposal, we supported the right of Quebec to participate in the selection of immigrants as set out in the Cullen-Couture Agreement. The reason being that we believe Quebec, more than the other provinces, has a special interest in protecting its linguistic character.
Our reading of the Constitution Act of 1982 is that the composition of the Supreme Court, that is, its size and the requirement that three of the nine judges be from Quebec, is already entrenched in the Constitution and can only be changed with the unanimous consent of the provinces. We therefore have no objection to spelling it out in more detail.
I have always believed that appointments to the court should be made after real consultation with national and provincial bar associations and, in the case of the Supreme Court of Canada, the provincial courts. I sincerely hope that the entrenchment of provincial consultation will enhance that process.
With regard to the spending power, the Government is introducing a new concept. It would enshrine in the Constitution the right of every province to reasonable compensation for not participating in a national cost-shared program in a provincial area, provided that the province has its own program which is compatible with national objectives.
Also, the statement of principles now provides that provinces will be reasonably compensated for opting out of any constitutional amendment affecting provincial jurisdiction, not just in areas of education or other cultural matters as is now the case under the Constitution Act of 1982.
We are very concerned that this dilution of the federal spending power could limit the ability of any future Canadian Government to initiate a national program on matters which generally fall within provincial jurisdiction.
We are deeply concerned, despite what the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) said this morning, that a medicare program might well have been impossible under the arrangement now contemplated. John Robarts, as the Premier of Ontario, was against that program, and under this provision he would have been able to block a national medicare system. We are
May 11, 1987

concerned that the national child care program might now be rendered impossible, as well as a guaranteed annual income. These are priorities for our Party.
Also, we are now assured by the Prime Minister that this Parliament will decide what is meant by a "national objective", but I think it is important that we understand how that process will come about. Will it be a parliamentary process or will it be left to the courts, with the Supreme Court of Canada being the final adjudicator? I suggest that the wording of this section needs to be very clear.
I will now deal with the amending formula. I am troubled by the rigidity in the new arrangement in terms of the unanimity required under the proposed amending process affecting federal institutions. We still believe that the 1971 Victoria formula is the best one, because it offers the necessary flexibility to face changing situations, while ensuring that regional interests and those of Quebec are fully protected.
By reverting to the unanimity rule on changes in the Senate and the addition of new provinces, are we not in effect moving backward rather than forward and ruling out any changes in those areas?
I think we are entitled to ask in the House whether we will ever have Senate reform in practical terms under these provisions. When I asked the Prime Minister last Monday if this provision meant that an elected Senate would now be impossible, he said, as reported at page 5684 of Hansard'.
Not unless you want to make the assumption that the First Ministers are
incapable of coming together in good faith to resolve matters of this kind.
I submit that the decades of constitutional impasse that we experienced in this country under that unanimity rule is precisely what we may experience now. We did not then have a workable amending formula. Constitutional reform was impeded because we had an implied unanimity rule. We should be seriously concerned that this particular change will move us backward to that situation prior to 1982.
The Prime Minister has conceded Senate appointments to the provinces until there is Senate reform, but there is no definition of what Senate reform might be. I suspect that some provincial Governments, having gained the power to appoint their own Senators and having guaranteed themselves yearly constitutional meetings with the Prime Minister, will be a lot less likely to move toward an elected Senate.
I am also concerned with the unanimity requirement for the admission of new provinces. While I agree that provinces should indeed have something to say about the admission of new ones, this rule did not apply to current provinces brought in after Confederation, the most recent being the Province of Newfoundland. Therefore, I believe an exception should be made in the case of Yukon and Northwest Territories and they should be governed by the current formula, seven provinces having 50 per cent of the Canadian population.
I am also very disappointed that the First Ministers did not seize the opportunity to recommit themselves to inserting the inherent rights of our aboriginal peoples into the Constitution.
The Constitution
As I said in the House prior to the meeting of First Ministers, and as indicated in our November amendment, we believe that the rights of our aboriginal peoples should be recognized in our Constitution.
Why did the First Ministers also not pursue the inclusion of a recognition of the multicultural nature of Canadian society? In particular, we must give due recognition to the many origins, creeds, cultures and different regional identities which shape our society. I suggest to the Prime Minister that we now have a unique opportunity to improve greatly and strengthen our Charter of Rights and Freedoms in two particular areas, as outlined in our resolution in November.

Mr. Speaker, we regret the fact that the Prime Minister of Canada did not take advantage of the favourable climate of the Meech Lake meeting to improve the scope of our Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms. We believe that he might have asked the provinces to grant official linguistic minorities the control and management of their publicly funded teaching institutions and to remove from the Charter, from the Constitution, the words "where the number so warrants" used in Section 23.
Hear, hear!

We would also like to take advantage of this opportunity to delete from Section 33 of our Constitution the word "notwithstanding" in order to give every Canadian man and woman throughout the country equal rights which can never be tampered with by any other level of government.

I would like to remind the House that under the terms of Section 33, the Legislatures in this country, including this Parliament, may limit, if they so choose, freedom of conscience and religion, of thought, belief, opinion, the press, peaceful assembly, association; and restrict the right to life, liberty and the security of the person; deny the right not to be arbitrarily arrested; waive due process of law; waive the right not to be subjected to cruel and unusual punishment and deny equal protection from discrimination based on race, national or ethnic origin, colour, religion, sex, age, or mental or physical disability.
I am sure most Hon. Members would like to see that provision removed, and I urge the Government to make its removal and the changes to Section 23 that I have just mentioned part of the current discussion with the provinces and with Parliament.
I repeat that 1 believe we have a historic opportunity to bring Quebec into our Constitution. We should take this opportunity to demonstrate to the people of Quebec that we want them in and we want them to play a significant and full partnership role in a better and more progressive Canada. It is what we all want in this country and what we have all been working for in this Parliament.

May 11, 1987
The Constitution
As I said at our November convention, Quebec on two recent occasions said yes to Canada. Now is an opportunity for this country and the House of Commons to say yes to Quebec.

Hear, hear!

Mr. Speaker, the historic meeting at Meech Lake with the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney), and the Premiers of all the other provinces, produced what can only be described as a remarkable document. I had the opportunity on that occasion, on behalf of my colleagues, to congratulate the Prime Minister and the Premiers for reaching an agreement, an agreement achieved by all of Canada's political parties representing all the regions of our country, and at this time obtaining the signature of the
Province of Quebec, which is something about which all Canadians should rejoice.
I made that statement at that time and I repeated it again to the Prime Minister. I added then on behalf of my colleagues simply the words, which I repeat, that we, of course, want to see the final wording -and the Prime Minister understands that-on some important clauses. However, the purpose, the general principles of what has been achieved, is something which should be endorsed by all Canadians in all regions of our land.
Today, rather than make a celebratory speech at this point, because I hope there will be another occasion before long when we have the final document before us, I have chosen to address a different kind of framework this morning.
I have chosen to try to lay out what I think would be the appropriate framework in which the House should put itself in assesssing a constitutional change and what that will mean or can mean for a nation, and then come quite specifically to some of the concessions in the document we have before us and raise certain areas of problematic concern with I hope will be addressed in a quite persuasive way by those who are now working on the final document.
Free societies are not those which seek unanimity. It is quite the contrary. Free societies are those which institutionalize conflicting opinion, reason and desire. Well functioning free societies are those in which these institutions, once established, contribute to a greater sense of harmony not merely for years but for decades and, indeed, for generations.

The opposing forces out of which harmony may result, in a country like ours, can unite to lay the foundation for durable harmony or they can do the exact opposite. They may succeed in creating no more than a temporary peace, a peace sought perhaps with a great deal of conviction but nevertheless, a peace that raises false hopes.
I believe that here in Canada, we must pay particular attention to this moment in our country's history, which we could call Phase II of the constitutional negotiations of the eighties.
I say this because I believe the Canadian people and our major political groups are all in favour of constitutional peace, which represents a tremendous opportunity for us in the short term. However, there is also a long-term risk involved for this country if we are not extremely careful. On the positive side, the fact is that the vast majority of the people of Quebec and those outside Quebec want the province to participate fully in the Canadian Constitution and to pursue its major role in shaping our national destiny. All the other provinces signed the Constitutional Accord in 1982. Only Quebec was excluded. We all know this situation is undesirable and that it must cease.
During the Referendum, Quebecers said yes to Canada. We now have a responsibility, here in the House of Commons and
May 11, 1987

in all the provinces, to say yes to Quebec. That is the reality today.
Hear, hear!

Mr. Speaker, we all know that the fundamental objective of the Meech Lake meeting was to develop a set of proposals that would satisfy Quebec's aspirations. However, these same proposals had to be acceptable to the other provinces, which have their own claims, and consistent with the need for the federal Government to maintain its power to ensure leadership in its quest for the unification of this country, not only in obtaining an agreement, but in meeting future responsibilities.
Unless I am sadly mistaken, I feel that virtually all political forces and Parties which thoroughly believe in a federal Canada share the same aspirations as the Canadian people. They are anxious for an agreement, as demonstrated at the Meech Lake meeting and here in the House of Commons the very next day.
All the political Parties representing the various Canadian regions have expressed the hope that once properly analyzed, the Meech Lake Agreement will satisfy the requirements of Canada, those of Quebec and those of all other provinces.
I said a week ago, Mr. Speaker, that my initial response to the document was positive, and it seems that the Meech Lake Agreement does indeed provide the requisite opening to the Province of Quebec. It does meet the concerns of other provinces, and it seems it does indeed maintain a strong unifying role for the federal Government.
In the final analysis, much depends upon the final wording of the text. The present wording, in certain key respects, I say frankly to the Prime Minister-and I suspect that he is aware of it and, as I understand it, many of the provincial Premiers are aware of it-in a number of particular sections, leaves much to be desired.
Today I want to talk about the wording used in two of the most important sections of the Agreement, the recognition of Quebec as a distinct society and the provision on the federal spending authority.

This is a happy moment in our history as we are about to recognize officially the unique character of Quebec society.
I am happy that the three federal political Parties have at last recognized this uniqueness one way or another.
The fact that the language and culture of most Quebecers are French not only enriches the life of that province, but represents a common wealth which all Canadian men and women may share. It is time for this uniqueness to be enshrined in the Canadian Constitution.
The Constitution
It is also important, however, that the vocabulary used be as precise as possible. Every time we add new elements to our Constitution, we are giving our courts a more active role to play.
In all fairness to our judges and the future generations of Canadians, we must give our courts the clearest direction possible. Otherwise, Mr. Speaker, they would have to create everything from scratch, and I do believe that the fundamental creative role in a democratic society should be played not by judges, but by politicians.

I come now to a particular case in point. Paragraph (l)(b) of the Accord notes, and I quote:
-that Quebec constitutes within Canada a distinct society.
In Clause (3) it stipulates that "the legislature and Government of Quebec" have a role to "preserve and promote the distinct identity of Quebec referred to in Paragraph (l)(b)".
The problem, Mr. Speaker, is that nowhere in Paragraph (l)(b) is a definition of "distinct society" to be found. There is simply the assertion that Quebec "constitutes ... a distinct society".
Surely those advocating the idea of distinctness had in mind the fact of the French-speaking majority and English-speaking minority in that province. Certainly, it is the view of my Party that the distinctness, the uniqueness, if you like, of the Province of Quebec is to be found in the fact that it is the only province in Canada in which the language and the culture of the majority is French, with the minority being English.
However, we differ, it seems to me, on other aspects of the Constitution. All three Parties in this House have now accepted, and accepted positively, this uniqueness, this specific quality of the Province of Quebec.
If that is the case, Mr. Speaker, it seems to me important that this be spelled out in the document we have before us. I believe it should be set out in Paragraph (l)(b) as part of the definition of the distinct character of the Province of Quebec.
I say this because it is essential that we send to the judges who will be asked to rule on the meaning of Clause (3) some message as to the meaning we had in mind.
If we do not do this, it seems to me to be entirely open to the judges to give paragraph (1) (b) almost any meaning they like. They may or may not refer back to paragraph (1) (a) for guidance, paragraph (1) (a) being that portion of the Accord which describes the linguistic majority being French in Quebec, with the minority being English speaking, and vice versa outside of the Province of Quebec.
Unless we provide some very specific definition with reference to the linguistic groups, those making judgments on the operative clause, Clause (3), will have no basis upon which to reach a decision about the meaning of the distinctiveness of Quebec, in respect of which a mandate is given to the Legislature of Quebec.

May 11, 1987
The Constitution
If we do not pin it down, the judges may well seize upon any particular definition they wish as to what the uniqueness and distinctiveness of Quebec is all about.
I do not want to be glib. The point is of fundamental importance in terms of constitutional law. We in this House do not want to leave open to the courts the opportunity to go burrowing about, only to find out that, in looking at a perhaps arcane aspect of the history of Quebec, it is some other consideration which they seize upon in giving definition to "distinctiveness" or "uniqueness". Therefore, I think we are obliged, in terms of giving positive force to what we all want to achieve-

Most francophones living in Quebec and most other Canadians living in other provinces accept the fact that this notion should be clearly defined in our Constitution.

It is for these reasons, Mr. Speaker, that I believe that clarification would be most usefully made in paragraph (l)(b), so that when a decision is rendered on Clause (3), the operative clause, the judges will at least have a bench-mark in assessing what we intended in saying that Quebec's legislature and Government have the authority to preserve and promote the distinct identity of Quebec.
It is for this reason I believe that the words "in that it is the only province with a French-speaking majority and an Englishspeaking minority", or words conveying the same idea should be added to the end of paragraph 1(b), so that the clause would then read:
(b) the recognition that Quebec constitutes within Canada a distinct society in that it is the only province with a French-speaking majority and an English-speaking minority.
I wish to stress, Mr. Speaker, that while they are specific words, what is important to me is not necessarily those specific words; what is important is that the idea contained therein be attached to Clause 1(b) so that the judges-not just the judges who are living with us now, but the judges in generations to come-will have a clear understanding of what we had in mind when we talked about the distinctiveness of the Province of Quebec.
I now turn to the federal spending power section of the Agreement. The wording of this section was intended to ensure the right of the Parliament of Canada to innovate, with its spending authority, new areas of policy with national programs thought to be of advantage to the whole country.
This has happened in the past, as we know very well, with medicare and hospitalization. At the same time, it is thought by modern federalists to be desirable, both from a constitutional distribution of powers point of view and from a recognition of the different circumstances in the different regions of our country, to allow, and indeed to encourage, provincial latitude in building such national programs.
Such can be done. That is, we can have effective programs nation-wide and at the same time have provincial decentralization. What is key is that the programs so established with regional variation are equivalent in their essential elements. If this is what the phrase "compatible with national objectives" means, then that is good and the people who got together at Meech Lake did a fine job.
However, once again it seems to me that the phrase used is subject to a judicial interpretation which could see a provincial program that is "compatible" with one established by the Parliament of Canada but falls short in a number of its details of what was intended by the Parliament of Canada.
If a program with five, six, or seven elements established by the Parliament of Canada, as I see it, is confronted with a province which wants to opt out and still receive compensatory financial assistance, it could provide a program with perhaps two or three elements only and, as we normally use the word, it could be compatible with the national program.
In replying to questions in the House of Commons last week, however, the Prime Minister-and I am pleased to note it- was as unequivocally clear as he was today when he spoke in affirming that it was the Parliament of Canada which would decide what were the national objectives that a province needed to be compatible with and to qualify for compensatory funding for its own program. Last week in the House the Prime Minister said: "with regard to who would set the national objectives, the Parliament of Canada". Again the Prime Minister said that a provincial program had to be "compatible with the national objectives set forth by this House".
I am pleased to see the Prime Minister and Deputy Prime Minister (Mr. Mazankowski) nodding affirmation and support of the idea once again today.
It is very important for today's Prime Minister to say this about today's agreement. However, I also believe-and I am sure the Prime Minister will not misunderstand-that it is much more important for the same idea to be found in wording in a Constitution which will hopefully be around long after we have long since departed this Chamber.
Hear, hear!

In short, it is more important for the future that this principle be included in the Constitution. Therefore, I think the following wording: "as established by the Parliament of Canada", which are the Prime Minister's own words, or their equivalent, should be added at the end of the existing wording in the clause. However, if the whole clause is now being rewritten to achieve this intent, we in this Party will of course find that acceptable.
Once again, the precise wording is not what my colleagues and I are after here. We are in pursuit of clear wording which
May 11, 1987

sends a clear constitutional message to Canadians today and to future generations of Canadians.
I took a little time on two important clauses in the resolution, because I thought at this stage in the proceedings, before we are confronted with a final document, it indeed is important for all participants in the process, including the Government of Canada, the provinces, and the opposition Parties, to make some constructive suggestions, and to put it very bluntly, including wording, at a time when it is perhaps a matter of just a few days before final documents can be circulated and discussed by the Premiers.
Obviously I want to say a few words about some other sections of this important document. I think the proposals on immigration are consistent with what has been done before in the Province of Quebec. It is now proposed to embed that in the Constitution, extending a similar right and principle to the other regions. It is a very constructive move.
Similarly, on the question of the Supreme Court, we in this Party believe that in a federal state there is a legitimate role to be played in the proposing of judges who will ultimately make decisions in interpreting the nature of the Constitution. We will have more things to say about that particular provision, but we certainly think that it is a move in the right direction.
On the question of other meetings, I think on the whole that the suggestion that the Prime Minister meet with the Premiers to talk about the fishery, Senate reform, and the economy are all important steps-it goes without saying. I simply want to add what I said the day after the Meech Lake Accord was reached. All Parties were represented there. I do not know what led to it or what factors were taken into consideration. I simply find it an unfortunate result that the people who came together with such seriousness of purpose, and seemed to achieve so much, left out the scheduling of, or specifically putting in the agreement for, meetings to deal with the aboriginal peoples of Canada.
To say the least, those of us who come from European ancestry or from many other parts of the world owe a great debt to the original people of the country which we now inhabit. I hope, at the next meeting to discuss the final wording of the document, that the Prime Minister and the Premiers will rethink the question of our obligation to the aboriginal peoples and will build into the agreement continuing meetings to discuss various issues-in particular the question of aboriginal self-government and the issue of comprehensive claims-with the aboriginal peoples until an agreement of some kind is reached.
I also want to say something on the question of the Northwest Territories and Yukon on which I had occasion to comment just after the Agreement. I want to say in the House what I said at that time. I think it regrettable that the Premiers and the Government of Canada have now decided to impose conditions on that part of Canada, our North, which were not applied to the other regions of Canada before they became provinces. With a little ingenuity-and it should not
The Constitution
take too much-and by looking at the operative clause, the Government of Canada and the provinces should be able to make an exemption and come back to at least the previous amending formula, which simply required seven provinces and 50 per cent of the population to make a decision about the possible bringing in on a provincial status of either the Northwest Territories or Yukon. I say that constructively, hoping that all the Premiers out there are listening to or will be reading this and that the Government of Canada will respond as well.
There is one section which I want to mention briefly, and that is the new amending formula. If there is one part which I think is almost irretrievably bad in this document, it is the new amending formula for federal institutions. Unlike the Prime Minister, I am not optimistic about the flexibility which will be permitted with this clause; in fact, quite the contrary. I do not normally indulge in Utopian politics, so I do not think there is much prospect for changing it. All those people came together and agreed on many other matters of great importance, and I suspect one of the conditions was that there was unanimous agreement and they came up with this formula. I regret to say that we will probably, to put it in pretty ordinary language, be stuck with it. All I can say is, thank God it does not apply to other parts of the Constitution.
However, perhaps there is some possibility of taking another look at the amending formula. I simply say on behalf of my colleagues, I am sure, and I would think on behalf of the majority of the people of Canada if they understood the implications of this very rigid formula, that the Premiers and Prime Minister should take another hard look at the amending formula. However I do not, I say candidly, anticipate that that will be done in this area.
I want to conclude in the way that I opened. It is a tough task to govern a nation, especially one like ours. It is a much greater task for those whose responsibility it is from time to time to charter the framework for future generations. We are embarked on that right now in this House and in the provinces. Although we need an agreement, and as a person who was here a few years ago and felt deeply that the Province of Quebec did not join in, I know I speak for all of us here on both sides when I say that one of the great joys of the accomplishment has been to see that the Government of the Province of Quebec has now decided to support and become a full participant in the constitutional process and, therefore, will reassume her important historical role. That is good.
Hear, hear!

I do want to say that all of us in this Chamber ought to have the occasion to look at the final wording of this important step in constitutional change. In fact, an extreme effort should be made for a non-partisan approach by us all to achieve the goals and principles which the Prime Minister addressed today, none of which we disagree with but positively support. Let us simply end up with

May 11, 1987
The Constitution
wording in the Constitution which carries out the very good intent that has been expressed in the Meech Lake document.
Hear, hear!

speakeroldname: Hon. Ray Hnatyshyn (Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada):
speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I am very proud and privileged to participate in this historic debate. Just before I get into my remarks, may I make some personal references that I believe are appropriate. I think this country owes a great debt of gratitude to the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) and the leadership he has shown in bringing together an accord which at last will bring Quebec into the mainstream of our country through the Constitution. That is not in any way to denigrate the role played by the provincial Premiers, which was also diplomatic, historic and very much in keeping with the sense of what I see in Canada today as a desire that we move together in unity with Quebec as an important part of our country.
Hear, hear!

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I say that as a western Canadian. I could not feel prouder about the role that was played by our Prime Minister. I could not feel prouder about the way in which all Premiers participated constructively.
I listened with great interest to the remarks of the Right Hon. Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Turner) and those of the Leader of the New Democratic Party, the Hon. Member for Oshawa (Mr. Broadbent). The message they gave was one of support for this proposition. It is a non-partisan issue, as they pointed out, and I believe that firmly. While there may be questions, suggestions and criticisms to approaches taken, I hope the discussion in the House will always be one of which we can be proud, and we can say that we moved Canada forward historically.
I understand there have been discussions between the House leaders of the Parties concerning the disposition of this motion. I think it important for us in this House to speak with a unified voice at the beginning of a very important process. For instance when the Prime Minister was Leader of the Opposition, almost in his first week here in this Chamber I recall, if I am not mistaken, he seconded a motion put forward by the Hon. Member for Winnipeg-Fort Garry (Mr. Axworthy) on behalf of the Liberal Government with respect to the Manitoba language issue. That to me was the essence of nonpartisanship. We were able to deal with that motion and have it accepted as part of the decisions of this House. I hope opposition Members will show the same sense of co-operation in this matter, particularly after they have declared themselves in favour and in support of this motion in principle. I do hope the discussions will carry on until six o'clock tonight.
My message today is a simple one. The Meech Lake Agreement constitutes a sound legal blueprint for the constitutional amendments now under consideration and for the further evolution of the Constitution, the fundamental law of this land.
The Meech Lake Agreement was unanimously supported by the 11 First Ministers and thus meets the strictest requirements of our Constitution's amending formula. All of the elements of the Agreement have been carefully examined from a legal and constitutional perspective. As Minister of Justice, I am fully satisfied that they constitute sound positive changes to the Constitution of Canada.

The Meech Lake Agreement is a major accomplishment which is in the best interest of all Canadians and marks the beginning of a new era for a Canadian federalism based on co-operation, harmony and mutual respect. This agreement is the result of an enormous collective effort on the part of the federal and provincial Governments.

We succeeded because of our willingness to recognize each other's legitimate concerns and to work toward a balanced resolution of those concerns. In this effort, it must be remembered that the First Ministers' meeting at Meech Lake was the culmination of a long process. It began in earnest with the Prime Minister's statement in Sept lies and with Quebec's clear statement of its constitutional conditions. Months of discussions and legal analysis built on that base.
The final agreement was not a last minute inspiration. It flowed directly from carefully constructed proposals that were well understood by all the participants. Everyone was satisfied that all legitimate interests had been taken into account and sufficiently protected. That is not to say, Mr. Speaker, that every possible application of the principles agreed upon can be clearly predicted with certainty. If that were possible, we would not need courts to help us resolve disputes when differing interpretations arise. Courts do play a central and critical role in federal systems of government. That is why it has been generally recognized for some time that the Supreme Court of Canada should be expressly entrenched in the Constitution. This is another major accomplishment that will be realized when the Meech Lake Agreement is implemented.
The entrenchment of the court will have the effect of clearly giving it constitutional status as the national court of ultimate appeal for Canada. This will highlight its status and function as the final, independent and impartial judicial arbiter of federal-provincial, citizen-state and private disputes of national importance. The Agreement also provides for entrenchment of the current statutory requirement that at least three of the nine justices appointed be from the Quebec bar. This is in continued recognition of Quebec's distinct civil law system. It ensures that the court will always have the necessary expertise to deal with civil law issues, whether they arise as pure matters of Quebec's internal civil law system or as an integral part of a broader public law issue.

Moreover, the agreement provides that, where there is a vacancy at the Supreme Court level, the federal Government
May 11, 1987

will appoint a person which it feels acceptable from a list of candidates proposed by the provinces.

This joint selection procedure provides for an important measure of provincial involvement which is appropriate for the court of last resort in a federal system. The agreement reached regarding the Supreme Court of Canada entrenches the court along with a new process for selection of candidates. This is in keeping with the nature of the court as an institution that must resolve questions relating to federal and provincial jurisdiction as well as important issues such as aboriginal rights and the scope of the rights and freedoms under the Charter.
In agreeing to share authority over the nomination process for Supreme Court judges, we believe we have acted wisely and in the best interests of the country, the court and indeed the Constitution. This reflects the new spirit of federalism which is visible throughout the Agreement. As a result, we shall strengthen the legitimacy of the court as the body which must adjudicate federal-provincial disputes and interpret the Charter of Rights for all Canadians.
As a western Canadian, I am particularly pleased that there will now be an ongoing opportunity in the constitutional context for a full and frank discussion of issues which are of concern to western Canadians. I am convinced that this process will ensure the institutional equality of all provinces within the Constitution.
In seeking this agreement with the full and essential participation of all the provinces, we all carried out the national will. We were not struggling against one another, we were struggling together to obtain something for our mutual benefit. There were no losers. The nation, with its strengthened constitutional fabric, is clearly the winner.
Hear, hear!

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I would like to say a word about the aboriginal peoples of Canada. In 1982, we recognized and affirmed the rights of the aboriginal peoples of Canada. We ensured that constitutional interpretation of the Charter be consistent with the preservation and enhancement of the multicultural heritage of Canadians.
The Governments committed themselves to promote equal opportunities to strengthen the regions of Canada, but one fundamental characteristic of Canada was not recognized in our Constitution. We had to come to the realization that the distinctiveness Quebec brings to Canada strengthens our identity and indeed our sovereignty. It is time we recognize this. As Victor Hugo once wrote, nothing in this world is so powerful as an idea whose time has come.
The Meech Lake Agreement provides for the recognition of this reality in a context that is perfectly appropriate for the political and legal challenges it is designed to meet. The elements of the provision were carefully drafted in an effort to
The Constitution
set out the reality of Canada and of Quebec within Canada without adversely affecting our traditional and fundamental constitutional arrangements. They will form part of the background against which the whole Constitution will be interpreted. It will ultimately be for the courts, and particularly for the Supreme Court of Canada to apply this new clause.
A sense of balance was also brought to bear on the other aspects of the Agreement. It is there in the elements of the agreement on immigration and spending power and indeed on the amending formula. The absence of Quebec from the constitutional process, an absence which very happily will be remedied by the agreement, has been a serious bar to the effective evolution of our Constitution. Constitutionally, we could probably not have effectively reformed the Senate without Quebec. Now we can and we will.
Hear, hear!

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
We will do it on the basis of an amending formula that recognizes the constitutional equality of all the provinces.
If unanimity was reached at Meech Lake, where six complex issues were on the table, it can and will be reached again. As the Prime Minister has pointed out, unanimity is not a strait-jacket. The Meech Lake Agreement will result in a constitutional requirement for an annual First Ministers' Conference to seek agreement on Senate reform, fisheries and other agreed upon matters. Those tasks should not be more difficult than the ones we are now completing.
While success in our future ventures is not necessarily guaranteed, success need not necessarily surprise us. It is within our capabilities, if we in fact preserve a sense of goodwill and a desire to build an even greater country.

Mr. Speaker, this agreement is perfectly consistent with our political traditions. We may use this opportunity to demonstrate how proud we are of it. We are convinced that the Canadian people will clearly understand the benefits of this new system.

The bold multicultural experiment called Canada continues not only to survive but to succeed. We know that there are many outstanding issues that still require our attention. As I indicated earlier, we have not forgotten nor will we ever forget matters of concern to aboriginal citizens or any of the other fundamentally important matters that will continue to merit our best efforts in the ongoing evolution of our country. Meetings continue to take place to develop a consensus in order to make progress in a constitutional sense in our commitment to these very important issues. It is with a full knowledge of the challenges ahead that I am confident the agreement we have reached will provide the constitutional bedrock for the country's future growth and development.

May 11, 1987
After the Meech Lake Agreement becomes part of our Constitution, we will have new institutional arrangements to foster greater federal-provincial co-operation and harmony. The challenge Canadian leaders will then face will be how best to make use of those new arrangements to serve the national interest and to ensure the general prosperity of all Canadians in all parts of the country.
I would like to conclude my remarks within the time allotted to me so that there can be full participation in this debate. There are certain areas each of us may wish had been dealt with at this time. However, I think it should not be lost on those of us who come from regions of Canada other than Quebec or Ontario that this Accord is probably the most important step forward in the recognition of regions like western Canada that has been passed in any constitutional amendment since Confederation, and 1 will tell you why, Mr. Speaker. It recognizes now that we are equals in Confederation.
Under this arrangement, we are equals with respect to important national institutions as opposed to what we would have been under previous proposals put forward, like the one referred to by the Right Hon. Leader of the Opposition. It was once proposed that the veto power should only lie with certain provinces, a proposal which in its time was of some attraction to the First Ministers. It had a very serious flaw, however, in that it absolutely left out western Canada. We have remedied that and 1 think the Prime Minister and the First Ministers should be applauded by all Canadians for recognizing that there are no second-class citizens in Canada.
Hear, hear!

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I would like to conclude by once again congratulating all the participants for the way they approached this matter. This is a time for leadership on the part of parliamentarians. 1 hope that we can work together at this time by supporting and passing this resolution, in whatever way possible agreed to among the House Leaders, in order to give the leadership that is required at this time in history. We must go forward and work in a constructive way with our ideas and suggestions for other constitutional matters and the matters before us at this time.
We welcome the opportunity to discuss these matters, whether it be through an Opposition day motion of which there are some 13 available to the Opposition in this time period, or with our own time. We have demonstrated that we are prepared to make this matter a priority by using a Government day for an important debate. I hope we will find new opportunities to debate this important issue in the House, and I say to all Hon. Members that I am very proud, not only to be a Member of this House but to be a Canadian at this time in history.
Hear, hear!
