subsubtopic: POLLUTION OF NIAGARA RIVER BY CHEMICALLY CONTAMINATED MIST
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, University of Toronto researchers estimate that as much as 60 tonnes a year of three chemicals, PCBs, chloroform, and chlorobenzenes, evaporate into the air from Niagara Falls. The total amount of chemicals released could be as high as 175 tonnes a year. According to the researchers, about half the chemicals come out of the mist at the Falls and the rest are released by wave action in the river.
In 1987 the Government reduced the strength of Environment Canada by 106 people. Since September, 1984, Environment Canada has lost S64 million in spending power to inflation.
Can the Government take any initiative to protect the health of Canadians living downwind of the Niagara River?
In November, 1984, the Government cancelled the funds necessary to develop the Guelph-Toronto Toxicology Centre intended to examine the threats posed to health and safety by toxic chemicals in the Great Lakes Basin. We call on the Government to reverse its decision of November, 1984, and give the green light to the establishment of the Guelph-Toronto Toxicology Centre to study this latest toxic threat to human health.
May 11, 1987

subtopic: TRIBUTE TO WORK OF POLICEMEN AND WOMEN-CALL FOR PUBLIC SUPPORT
TRIBUTE TO WORK OF POLICEMEN AND WOMEN-CALL FOR PUBLIC SUPPORT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in recognition of Police Week I would like to draw the attention of the House to the excellent police services provided to Canadians. We are all extremely fortunate and grateful for the competence, dedication and fairness shown by Canada's policemen and women. At the same time I would like to remind Hon. Members and all Canadians that crime control is everybody's business.
We all have a responsibility and a capacity to assist Canada's police forces in maintaining the peace and combating crime in our communities. While Police Week provides a special opportunity to show our appreciation to Canada's police forces, I am hopeful that each of us and our constituents will take this opportunity to explore with our respective police forces the ways in which we can assist in preserving peace and order in our communities.

subtopic: OPPOSITION OF NATIONAL ACTION COMMITTEE ON THE STATUS OF WOMEN
OPPOSITION OF NATIONAL ACTION COMMITTEE ON THE STATUS OF WOMEN
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this past week-end delegates to the 15th annual general meeting of the National Action Committee on the Status of Women, Canada's largest women's organization representing over 500 groups from coast-to-coast, spoke out strongly against the return of capital punishment. Their resolution notes that capital punishment is legislated murder by the state and is the ultimate in violence.
These same women voice their deep concern at the possibility that the motion shortly to be voted on standing in the name of the Hon. Member for Grey-Simcoe (Mr. Mitges) entrenching the rights of the foetus in the Constitution poses a profound threat to Canadian women. The sponsor of this motion has said that women seeking abortions in Canada whose lives are not threatened, and the doctor who performs the abortion, should be charged with murder and executed. That is shameful.
Let us join with the women of Canada and Members of Parliament like the Hon. Member for Lisgar (Mr. Murta) and the Hon. Member for Bourassa (Mr. Rossi) who have shown great courage in this debate in rejecting their earlier position on this issue and the cry for a return to the death penalty.

subtopic: YOUTH SCIENCE FOUNDATION-SPONSORSHIP OF SCIENCE FAIRS
YOUTH SCIENCE FOUNDATION-SPONSORSHIP OF SCIENCE FAIRS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, during the past month the Youth Science Foundation has sponsored 85 regional science fairs across Canada, including one in Ottawa-Carleton. The innovation and creativity demonstrated by the more than 400,000 young Canadians who participated is most impressive.
The 400 regional winners meet this week at the CanadaWide Science Fair at Erindale College in Mississauga to compete for national honours. Some of Canada's future scientific leaders will be among the participants.
The Youth Science Foundation seeks to promote an appreciation and understanding of science in every young Canadian. It encourages young people to pursue careers in science and technology. It helps to develop the great potential Canada has through its youth to become an international leader in science and technology.
The Youth Science Foundation is supported in part by the federal Government and is important to all Canadians because of the manner in which it develops the skills of young Canadians.

Mr. Speaker, education, particularly post-secondary education, is an investment in the future. The link between higher educational attainment and better employment and economic development opportunities is undeniable. Why, then, is the Government cutting back on post-secondary education for those for whom the benefits are needed most and who would reap the greatest results? I refer to the Indian people of Canada.
Study after study has documented the social, economic and educational disparities between Indians and non-Indians in this country. In recent years more and more Indian students have been staying in school and returning to school and they are graduating. Yet the Government has decided to stem this growth in achievement. It has limited its post-secondary program, capped the number of students it will sponsor, and restricted resources to Indian educational institutions.
Under the previous Government the principles of universal access and opportunity prevailed. This Government has crushed those principles and once again deficit reduction is occurring on the backs of those least able to bear it.

May 11, 1987

speakerposition: Chief Government Whip's assistant; Deputy Whip of the Progressive Conservative Party
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this Conservative Government always favoured the creation of long-term jobs. Since we came to power, the Canadian economy has been constantly improving. We gave private enterprise the tools needed for its economic recovery. Interest rates went down, major investment projects were set up across the land, and the hope of soon having access to a new, 250-million people market stimulates Canadian entrepreneurs.
Mr. Speaker, Statistics Canada's figures for April, 1987 show the unemployment rate is at its lowest in five years. Canadians have elected a Government that is building a strong, healthy economy that will make our native land the land of our children.

subtopic: NATIONAL ACTION COMMITTEE DELEGATES' LETTERS TO PRIME MINISTER
NATIONAL ACTION COMMITTEE DELEGATES' LETTERS TO PRIME MINISTER
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, yesterday delegates wrote many letters to the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) including the following:
The Government's decision to ignore the long-scheduled lobby of the National Action Committee on the Status of Women reinforces the public perception that anything is more important than the concerns of women in Canada.

Is this your idea of giving priority to women's issues? Your Government does not respect its commitment to women of all ages.

This lack of respect for and commitment to our representations will not be tolerated.

I am nine years old .... I feel very sad about the fact that you do not listen to my granny and all the other women that wanted to talk to you tomorrow.
A further letter reads:
I can no longer believe that you will honour your commitments or promises . .. . A disappointed potential supporter-
Yet another reads:
NAC represents more than 3 million voting women in Canada-we have the right to be heard and treated with respect.

subtopic: RECOMMENDATION THAT STUDENTS REGISTER AT CANADA EMPLOYMENT CENTRES AS SOON AS POSSIBLE
RECOMMENDATION THAT STUDENTS REGISTER AT CANADA EMPLOYMENT CENTRES AS SOON AS POSSIBLE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to urge students who are looking for summer jobs to apply as soon as possible to Manpower Canada's student centres. Again this year, through Challenge 87, this Government will create 90,000 jobs in Canada, 25,000 of which are in Quebec. That program's goal remains very clear. It is to make easier for young people the transition to the workplace. Those jobs are financially interesting and allow them to get job training and experience. For example, the Department of National Defence will be in a position to offer jobs to 7,000 students in Canada, 1,606 of which in Quebec.
I remind that Manpower Canada's student centres help students find jobs and allow employers to hire workers during the summer season. Last summer, more than 425,000 students across Canada were placed that way.
In conclusion, I wish good luck to all students in their search for a job, and I remind them to apply now!

subtopic: BANFF NATIONAL PARK-OPPOSITION TO SUNSHINE VILLAGE EXPANSION
BANFF NATIONAL PARK-OPPOSITION TO SUNSHINE VILLAGE EXPANSION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, earlier today the Minister of the Environment (Mr. McMillan) met with representatives of the Canadian Environmental Network. During that meeting many concerned environmentalists called on the Minister to reject proposals by the Sunshine Village ski resort to expand beyond its current lease area inside Banff National Park. I want to reiterate the NDP's opposition to this expansion.
To allow Sunshine's proposed expansion to go ahead would fly in the face of the 1978 decision to establish Sunshine's current lease area and limit further expansion. It would fly in the face of Parks Canada policy and it would fly in the face of In Trust for Tomorrow: A Management Framework for Four Mountain Parks which the Minister published last year.
In addition, any expansion of Sunshine Village would make a mockery of the Minister's proposed amendments to the National Parks Act to limit such areas within national parks. Most important, Sunshine's proposal, particularly plans to increase summer use dramatically, could destroy Sunshine Meadows which Parks Canada has identified as one of the most threatened areas in Banff National Park.
Too often in the past Parks Canada policy has been altered or simply ignored to serve short-term political or economic
May 11, 1987

expediency. EIow the Minister deals with the Sunshine Village expansion proposal will be an important test of the Minister's personal commitment and that of the Conservative Government to protect and preserve our national parks.

subtopic: RECOGNITION OF QUEBEC AS DISTINCT SOCIETY
RECOGNITION OF QUEBEC AS DISTINCT SOCIETY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on the very first Canada Day in 1867, the Quebec newspaper La Minerve said: "The new Constitution recognizes the French Canadians as a distinct and separate nationality. We constitute a state within a state. We enjoy the full exercise of our rights and the formal recognition of our national independence".
By recognizing Quebec as a distinct society, by giving it and other provinces a first right of refusal over changes in the House of Commons, Senate and Supreme Court of Canada, by limiting the federal spending power in areas of provincial jurisdiction, and by giving the provinces a formal voice in immigration policy and Supreme Court of Canada appointments, the Meech Lake Accord has acknowledged and confirmed the principles set out in La Minerve in 1867. Those are principles on which Quebec understood that it had entered Confederation in the first place. Those principles have had their opponents in the past and they still have them today, but without those principles there would be no Canada.

Mr. Speaker, society has changed dramatically in the past 20 years. Today, less than one in six Canadian families fits the traditional family pattern of the wife at home with the children and the husband out working. Many families are headed by single parents, most of whom are young mothers.
Inadequate child care is not just a woman's issue. It is not just an issue for parents. It is an issue for all of us, including parents, employers, Governments-all Canadians. I believe that all of us have a responsibility and a duty to be part of the solution.
We in the Liberal Party believe that an adequate, affordable, accessible, quality child care system must be based on two principles: sharing the burden, and providing choices for the pre-schooler as well as the latchkey school-aged child.
Our Party has put forward a realistic and responsible solution in the Liberal pocket paper on child care which can be
obtained from our office or the office of the Member for Outremont (Mrs. Pepin).
Liberals view child care as a support to good parenting, not a substitute for it. In our program, the parent's role is paramount. It is time that the federal Government showed some leadership on this issue.

subtopic: EMPLOYMENT EQUITY-GOVERNMENT'S EMPHASIS ON TRAINING FOR WOMEN
EMPLOYMENT EQUITY-GOVERNMENT'S EMPHASIS ON TRAINING FOR WOMEN
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, once again I want to emphasize to the House the great importance that the Government places on the achievement of economic equality for women. A major step forward in this regard occurred last November at the First Ministers' Conference in Vancouver. At that time, the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) and Premiers endorsed a labour force strategy which has a particular emphasis on training for women. Next month, federal, provincial and territorial Ministers responsible for the status of women will be meeting with Ministers responsible for labour market matters to elaborate on this strategy.
Our Government is also addressing women's employment needs through the Canadian Jobs Strategy. For the first time ever, our national employment and training strategy includes targets for the participation of women and a particular emphasis on women re-entering the job market. These two measures, along with many others introduced by the Government, will go a long way to promote the full participation of women in all sectors of economic activity.

subtopic: VANCOUVER GROUP'S OPPOSITION TO PROPOSED LEGISLATION
VANCOUVER GROUP'S OPPOSITION TO PROPOSED LEGISLATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, over the week-end in Vancouver I met with a group called The Coalition on Pornography. It is made up of representatives of the Anglican Church, University Women's Club, Justice Institute, the Junior League, the North Shore Women's Centre, and the Periodical Review Board.
This group was formed to fight pornography and get the Government to bring forward legislation against it. Ironically, they now find themselves fighting the legislation because it goes too far and has, in effect, as its basic premise, that all sex is dirty. I want to bring their representations to the House and urge the Government to bring forward reasonable legislation that combats real pornography but recognizes that sexuality is a part of life in Canada.

May 11, 1987
Oral Questions

Mr. Speaker, our country has everything to gain from the full participation of women in the various aspects of Canadian society. That is why when we came to power, and because of the urgent need to act, our Government agreed to double from 15 per cent to 30 per cent the number of women on the various federal boards, commissions and offices.
In the Throne Speech of October 1, 1986, we confirmed our intention to increase the participation of women in the various stages of the decision making process. And the figures are there to show that we are living up to our commitment to Canadian women.
Only half-way through our mandate, over 27 per cent of all the Government's discretionary appointees have been women. By appointing a greater number of women to key positions, the Government wants to show the way to the private sector and the Canadian people generally.

subtopic: CHARTERED BANKS OPPOSED TO UNIONIZATION OF EMPLOYEES
CHARTERED BANKS OPPOSED TO UNIONIZATION OF EMPLOYEES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, 1 believe it is time that we changed the Canada Labour Code with respect to the certification of employees who wish to become members of a union. Some of the major employers in this country which have made huge profits, namely, the banks, also pay low taxes. They have been very successful in preventing their employees from organizing into unions. Most of these employees are women and receive low salaries despite the fact the banks make high profits and pay low taxes.
When there have been attempts by these workers to organize, the banks have used every means at their disposal to make sure these workers do not become part of a union. Time after time the Canadian Labour Relations Board has ruled against the banks but the end result is that these people do not get to remain in unions. I believe that is one reason these people receive low salaries, which helps to create the spread between male workers and female workers.
It is time the Government conducted an investigation into this matter and ensured we have a labour code which adequately protects the rights of female workers.

subtopic: CEREMONIAL ROUTE-ABANDONMENT OF PLAN TO USE COLOURED PAVING
CEREMONIAL ROUTE-ABANDONMENT OF PLAN TO USE COLOURED PAVING
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Government has shown one more time how it can be weak-kneed when confronted with even a slight bit of controversy. A few days ago the National Capital Commission announced it no longer intended to proceed with the planned coloured repaving of the designated ceremonial route in the Ottawa area. Since the NCC had repeatedly affirmed its commitment to this project in the past, I have concluded that its change of heart was caused by none other than the Deputy Prime Minister (Mr. Mazankowski) responding to the whining and moaning of a few disgruntled backbench Tory Members of Parliament.
With this kind of weak-kneed approach, our national railways, our government-run airlines and even the construction of our War Memorial would have never proceeded. The Parliament Buildings would probably have never been built. The National Capital area is being very poorly served by the present Tory Government. They shall remember.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. John N. Turner (Leader of the Opposition):
subsubtopic: REQUEST FOR ASSURANCE TAX WILL NOT BE IMPOSED ON FOOD
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, single mothers and, indeed, many Canadian families are having difficulty putting food on the table these days. Over the past week-end, the National Action Committee on the Status of Women at its meetings here in Ottawa expressed grave reservations about the possibility of a national sales tax on food as well as a tax on other necessities.
My question is a simple one. Will the Prime Minister do a very simple thing right now and assure Canadians that there will never be a national sales tax on food?

subsubtopic: REQUEST FOR ASSURANCE TAX WILL NOT BE IMPOSED ON FOOD
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I was absent when the Minister of Finance addressed this matter in the House in the last couple of days. However, in regard to the spirit of tax reform, the idea is a greater degree of fairness for Canadians in the tax system in a very special way, a greater degree of fairness for those on the lower levels of the income scale and a greater degree of relief for them and their parents, including the individuals to whom the Right Hon. Leader of the Opposition referred.
The details of this will be spelled out when the White Paper is published on June 18. My right hon. friend, as a former Minister of Finance, will, of course, want to wait for the publication of that document.
May 11, 1987

subsubtopic: REQUEST FOR ASSURANCE TAX WILL NOT BE IMPOSED ON FOOD

subtopic: CENTRES FOR BATTERED WOMEN AND THEIR CHILDREN- PRIME MINISTER'S POSITION

speakeroldname: Right Hon. John N. Turner (Leader of the Opposition):
subtopic: CENTRES FOR BATTERED WOMEN AND THEIR CHILDREN- PRIME MINISTER'S POSITION
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, Canadian women have learned that they can no longer rely on the Prime Minister's word. In the Speech from the Throne, the Government had promised once more to address the immediate and long-term problems of battered women and their children. Instead, existing shelters for battered women throughout Canada have had to close down because of the budgetary cutbacks in spending and the lack of a national social housing program. When is the Prime Minister going to keep his word in this respect?

speakeroldname: Hon. Jake Epp (Minister of National Health and Welfare):
speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
subtopic: CENTRES FOR BATTERED WOMEN AND THEIR CHILDREN- PRIME MINISTER'S POSITION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in response to the question of the Right Hon. Leader of the Opposition, the Prime Minister is keeping his word. One need only look to the changes made to the Canada Assistance Plan.
While that plan was based on financial need, as he will be aware, the argument we put forward is that persons could have needs other than financial, and the plan has been expanded. There has been close co-operation between the federal Government and the provinces in that respect.

subtopic: CENTRES FOR BATTERED WOMEN AND THEIR CHILDREN- PRIME MINISTER'S POSITION
speechtext: Let me say to the Minister that on Friday last I was in contact with the Downtown East Side Women's Centre, and certainly his programs are not evident at that particular centre, or other centres for battered women in Vancouver. I hope there will be some action on this.

speakeroldname: Hon. Jake Epp (Minister of National Health and Welfare):
speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I do not want to leave any wrong impression that the provinces are not co-operating. In fact, quite the opposite is taking place. There is very close co-operation in the discussions between the provinces and our federal responsibility.
I accept what the Hon. Member says in terms of the urgency. The Prime Minister has very clearly indicated that. He has put his personal imprimatur on it. It is that mandate that we are following.

subsubtopic: TELEVISION-PARTICIPATION OF WOMEN AT PRODUCTION LEVEL
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, broadcasting has the power to shape attitudes, values, and provide role models for our children. However, according to recent statistics, men outnumber women two to one as prominent television characters in prime time programming and four to one in children's programming. Not only are
May 11, 1987

women under-represented, they are often misrepresented on television, performing a limited number of stereotyped roles.
My question is for the Minister of Communications. Will the Minister introduce broadcasting legislation to increase the number of women at the production level as well as on the screens of the Canadian broadcasting system, so that there will be a fairer portrayal on Canadian airwaves?

subsubtopic: TELEVISION-PARTICIPATION OF WOMEN AT PRODUCTION LEVEL
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as the Hon. Member fully knows, we are in the midst of reviewing the Broadcasting Act and preparing for the introduction of new legislation. She is one of the hard-working members of the committee. I take her representations at this time as something to be considered as we come forward with a new Broadcasting Act.
I also want to mention that the CRTC has recently put forward guidelines for sex role stereotyping which should also be considered in the revision of the Broadcasting Act.

subtopic: APPLICATION OF EMPLOYMENT EQUITY ACT-ROLE OF CRTC
APPLICATION OF EMPLOYMENT EQUITY ACT-ROLE OF CRTC
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my supplementary question is directed to the same Minister. Notwithstanding the important step forward in terms of sex role stereotyping, I would like a stronger statement of commitment, if possible.
Since the current Employment Equity Act lacks an effective enforcement mechanism, will the Minister ensure that employment equity obligations apply to all broadcasting licencees regardless of size and that the CRTC is mandated to supervise and enforce employment equity provisions as a condition of licence?

subtopic: APPLICATION OF EMPLOYMENT EQUITY ACT-ROLE OF CRTC
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I was very pleased to see that in a recent rulings of the CRTC it did make compliance with the guidelines on sex role stereotyping one of the conditions of licence when the application comes forward for renewal.
I think there are advances in this field, and I am very pleased with the way in which the broadcasting community is addressing itself to the provisions of the present Employment Equity legislation in order to ensure greater equality in our broadcasting industry for women and for minority groups.

My question is for the Minister for National Health and Welfare. It has to do
Oral Questions
with child care concerns raised by the National Action Committee on the Status of Women. The Minister knows that study after study has shown that non-profit child care is consistently of higher quality than commercial child care.
Will the Minister put aside his own market-place ideology and assure the women of Canada that their children will not be used for profit and that new public funds for child care will go to develop non-profit child care services?

speakeroldname: Hon. Jake Epp (Minister of National Health and Welfare):
speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the Hon. Member puts forward an argument which she knows does not do any justice to families who decide what type of child care they want, whether it is non-profit, commercial, or informal child care. Hear, hear!

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext: What I promise the Hon. Member and the House is that when the Government puts forward its proposal there will be a wide range of choices, which I think is an approach more in keeping with what Canadian parents want.
Mr. Speaker, we are talking about the appropriate use of tax dollars for child care. Appropriate use is not for profit-making child care.

Another related overriding concern of women is the quality of child care, Mr. Speaker. They are very concerned that the Minister may extend or agree to extend Canada Assistance Plan funding. Will the Minister guarantee that the Canada Assistance Plan funding, which is a welfare program-we want child care to be for everybody-will not be extended to fund profit-making child care either now or in the future?

speakeroldname: Hon. Jake Epp (Minister of National Health and Welfare):
speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare

Mr. Speaker, again the Hon. Member forgets, for example, that the present Ontario Government recognizes that over 50 per cent of its spaces are in the very types of configuration which she condemns; in Alberta around 70 per cent are and, in Atlantic Canada, which does not have the kind of financial resources that some of the other provinces have, the percentage is also very high. Simply to condemn, then to lose those spaces and to say we have done more for child care is to argue the preposterous. What I am saying to the Hon. Member is what I said in my first answer, that there will be a choice, and she will have to wait for that day.

May 11, 1987
Oral Questions PORNOGRAPHY

Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Minister of Justice. It concerns Bill C-54, the pornography Bill. When the Government began to encounter criticism of the Bill the Minister suggested that he would be flexible and would accept constructive amendments to it. Over the week-end, the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs in Calgary suggested that the Bill could not please everybody and that the Government would move ahead with it.
Was the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs speaking for the Government or is the Government prepared to accept constructive amendments to get away from this idea that all sexuality is pornography?

speakeroldname: Hon. Ray Hnatyshyn (Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada):
speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I appreciate the question on this important Bill. I think that I have to take issue with the Hon. Member's generalization about the legislation. His generalization is just the opposite from the actual fact.
If the Member reads the Bill, he will see that we have attempted to bring a balance with respect to this whole question. I do not believe that there is anyone in the House who thinks it is an easy proposition to define these matters. I can tell the Hon. Member that this Bill is light years ahead of present law and it is receiving very substantial support across the country.
His own Party has been calling for strong legislation on pornography and the importation of this type of material into our country. I hope the Member will not change the policy of his own Party in order to carry out the wishes of the editorial board of The Toronto Star.

subtopic: REQUEST THAT GOVERNMENT DIVIDE BILL IN TWO
REQUEST THAT GOVERNMENT DIVIDE BILL IN TWO
speechtext: I have a supplementary, Mr. Speaker. I should like to ask the Minister whether he would be prepared-because it is true that the Liberal Party supports such a legislation-to bring forward a Bill dealing with violence, degradation, child pornography and leave aside that encroachment on Canadian life standards; in other words, is he prepared to divide the Bill, to introduce legislation dealing with the parts on which we agree and waive the remainder pending a more thorough study?

speakeroldname: Hon. Ray Hnatyshyn (Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada):
speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: REQUEST THAT GOVERNMENT DIVIDE BILL IN TWO
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I do not quite understand what the Hon. Member is saying. He knows what the present state of the law is. The highest courts have determined that depictions as I have set forth in this legislation are currently considered to be obscene under the present law. If the Hon. Member is suggesting that we want to expand and loosen the present standards to allow for pornography to be available in
the corner confectionery stores across the country and in various neighbourhoods, I wish he would stand up and say so.
I think it is important to put this in perspective. I appreciate constructive suggestions. I would be prepared to listen to them but, on the other hand, I do not want generalizations which are inaccurate to be the basis of those suggestions.

subtopic: POSITION OF NATIONAL ACTION COMMITTEE ON THE STATUS OF WOMEN
POSITION OF NATIONAL ACTION COMMITTEE ON THE STATUS OF WOMEN
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, my question is also for the Minister of Justice. This past week-end the National Action Committee on the Status of Women, Canada's largest women's group, voted overwhelmingly to reject the Government's proposed Bill on pornography. Will the Minister now agree to scrap this dangerous and Victorian legislation? Will the Minister bring forward instead a Bill which clearly distinguishes between violent and exploitive degrading pornography on the one hand and images of consensual adult sexuality on the other, as strongly recommended by the Fraser Commission? Will the Minister not understand that basic distinction, Mr. Speaker?

speakeroldname: Hon. Ray Hnatyshyn (Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada):
speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: POSITION OF NATIONAL ACTION COMMITTEE ON THE STATUS OF WOMEN
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I do not take issue with the resolutions that have been passed. People have different points of view. The President of the National Action Committee on the Status of Women on the tabling of this legislation I thought had a very supportive statement when she asked this House to move quickly on this important legislation. This legislation, I think, represents a balanced approach. It is in accordance with the values and traditions which the overwhelming majority of Canadians hold respecting acceptable material.
If the Hon. Member has suggestions about the Bill, I would like to hear them, I think at committee stage, but I do not want to take his generalization that we should simply open the doors and have no provisions at all with respect to pornography. I do not think that is a fair position for the New Democratic Party to take, quite frankly.

Mr. Speaker, the President of NAC speaks for her organization in overwhelmingly rejecting this legislation.
The Minister has said that images of caring relationships will not be affected by this Bill, and yet the definition of erotica in the Bill includes only nudity and nothing more. Does this mean that for a Tory Government a caring relationship is an exclusively non-sexual relationship? Why has the Government rejected the Fraser Commission's recommendation, that the Government has no right to invade the bedrooms of the nation to tell adults that they cannot view consensual adult sexual activity? Why this puritanical anti-sex approach, Mr. Speaker?
May 11, 1987

subsubtopic: LACK OF SUFFICIENT HOUSES ON RESERVES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Minister of Employment and Immigration. Is the Minister aware that many Canadian native women who have had their Indian status restored as a result of Bill C-31 are unable to return to their communities because there are not enough houses? Housing construction in Indian communities has nearly been paralysed because of the Minister's refusal to use the Jobs Strategy Program to provide the labour component of the construction of houses.
Oral Questions
Is the Minister prepared now to tell the House that he will adjust his policy so that Indian women and their children who want to go home will be able to find houses when they do so?

speakeroldname: Hon. Benoit Bouchard (Minister of Employment and Immigration):
subsubtopic: LACK OF SUFFICIENT HOUSES ON RESERVES
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the question raised by my colleague was drawn to my attention some time ago. Moreover, I have met with the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development on two or three occasions. However, my colleague should know that funds earmarked for the Canadian employment strategy are distributed in an equitable fashion among various Canadian groups and generally speaking, native people have received sums corresponding to their needs. However, I recognize with him that the training problem and the implementation of the employment strategy represent a special problem in the case of native people since on reserve training and even off reserve training gives rise to a particular problem. This issue is now under consideration and I shall be in a position to give an answer in that respect in the days or weeks to come.

subtopic: CANADIAN JOBS STRATEGY-USE OF FUNDS FOR INDIAN COMMUNITIES
CANADIAN JOBS STRATEGY-USE OF FUNDS FOR INDIAN COMMUNITIES
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the Minister knows that Indian communities lost $8 million from what they had under the Canada Works Program because of the change in his policy. Will the Minister confirm to the House that his colleague, the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development, made a very specific request, having recognized the gravity of this situation, for a fair share of the Canadian Jobs Strategy funds so that Indian communities can have houses built now when the construction season is getting under way? Will the Minister confirm that he received that request and will he tell the House that he is prepared to respond to that request quickly and positively?

speakeroldname: Hon. Benoit Bouchard (Minister of Employment and Immigration):
subtopic: CANADIAN JOBS STRATEGY-USE OF FUNDS FOR INDIAN COMMUNITIES
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I told my friend that I met with the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development two or three times. The requests of the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development are always fair, but I am not ready today to say when I will be ready to give that answer. It will be a good and a fair answer but we have to take into account that this money has to be expended with fairness for all Canadians.

subsubtopic: BUSINESS TRANSFER TAX-OPPOSITION OF NATIONAL ACTION COMMITTEE ON THE STATUS OF WOMEN
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I address my question to the Prime Minister and it is with reference to his statement that the new sales tax and tax reform will be

May 11, 1987
Oral Questions
fair. He knows that the National Action Committee on the Status of Women representing three million Canadians has declared its unequivocal opposition to proposals for a business transfer tax or some other form of sales tax that would impose a tax on essentials such as food because of the impact it would have on working families and on poor families, most of which are headed by women.
Could the Prime Minister clarify the confusion left by the Minister of Finance last week and tell us specifically if the Minister of Finance was reflecting government policy when he said that only low-income families would receive some kind of a sales tax credit to offset this proposed new sales tax on food?

subsubtopic: BUSINESS TRANSFER TAX-OPPOSITION OF NATIONAL ACTION COMMITTEE ON THE STATUS OF WOMEN
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, last week the Minister of Finance indicated that the Government of Canada would be setting out its views in regard to tax reform in a White Paper on June 18. He indicated the components of that and the philosophy behind it. That philosophy is one of greater fairness, the elimination of tax avoidance, and a greater degree of fairness and assistance for those who are at the lowest level of the income pole. This will be accomplished in a number of ways, all of which will be set out in the White Paper to be presented on June 18. My hon. friend would no doubt want to wait until he sees the integrated package before he asks me to comment on any hypothesis.

Mr. Speaker, is the Prime Minister aware of the fact that the existing sales tax credit, modest as it is, is given only to families earning less than $17,000 per year and therefore not only excludes large numbers of working families just above the poverty line but also excludes many thousands of families that are actually below the poverty line? Is this the model for the proposed sales tax credit on food? Does this not mean that the Government intends to make working families pay this sales tax on food of $300 per year while many families in poverty will pay the sales tax as well? Is that his policy?
No.
Hear, hear!

Hon. Warren Allmand (Notre-Dame-de-Grace-Lachine
East): Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Minister of Employment and Immigration. There have been reports that the Minister has now decided not to proceed with any reform of the Unemployment Insurance Act despite unanimous recommendations to the contrary made by the Standing Committee on Labour, Employment and Immigration. Is that
correct? Is it true that the Minister has now dropped any reform of the Unemployment Insurance Act?

speakeroldname: Hon. Benoit Bouchard (Minister of Employment and Immigration):
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the other day my colleague, the Hon. Member for Nickel Belt, said that we do have a reform of $1 billion. I told him that he did not have good information. Today I told my friend that there will be an announcement next Friday on unemployment insurance reform.

Hon. Warren Allmand (Notre-Dame-de-Grace-Lachine
East): Mr. Speaker, while there were some differences between the Standing Committee report and the Forget report, there were also some major grounds of agreement including what should be done with maternity benefits and parental benefits. Would the Minister not at least legislate in those areas where there is agreement between the two reports?

speakeroldname: Hon. Benoit Bouchard (Minister of Employment and Immigration):
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the Government has received and will continue to receive a number of reports on a problem as special as unemployment insurance. There is no question of the Government considering only one aspect of a report. We have to define whether the current unemployment insurance system is now meeting the needs of Canadians. And in accordance with the reviews which will be made and reports which we have received, we will table next Friday what the Government intends to do about unemployment insurance.

subsubtopic: PROPOSED SALE OF CADILLAC FAIRVIEW TO UNITED STATES FIRM
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, my question is directed to the Prime Minister. Just weeks after the Dome sale was announced, another large Canadian firm, Cadillac Fairview, is now being sold to a U.S. firm, putting malls and office buildings right across the country in U.S. hands. What does the Government intend to do to promote the Canadianization of the economy and to reverse this growing shift to U.S. control of key firms across the economy?

speakeroldname: Hon. Michel Cote (Minister of Regional Industrial Expansion):
subsubtopic: PROPOSED SALE OF CADILLAC FAIRVIEW TO UNITED STATES FIRM
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the first thing I want to tell my colleague is that the company concerned did not submit an application to Investment Canada. Besides, when reviewing such applications, we always make sure, before anything else, that Canadian interests are protected, and they have been in those instances, when we take into account the Canadian participation in the management of that corporation; second,
May 11, 1987

the increase in Canadian productivity and third, the technology ownership.
That is how, each time we review such transactions, we look after Canadians' interests.

Mr. Speaker, I would point out to the Minister that this firm has even refused to sell public shares to Canadians. I hope that will be part of what his review will look at.
Will the Minister assure Canadians that the Investment Canada review that will take place will permit communities right across the country to have input on this takeover since these changes in ownership will be of such importance to those communities and the country itself?

speakeroldname: Hon. Michel Cote (Minister of Regional Industrial Expansion):
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I will only repeat what I said. Every time we have to review such transactions-and since the enactment of the new legislation on Investment Canada, that corporation has reviewed more than 2,200 of them-we have always safeguarded Canadians' interests and we will continue to do so, Mr. Speaker.

subsubtopic: WHEAT FARMERS-1987-88 CROP YEAR-REQUEST FOR DEFICIENCY PAYMENT
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, my question is directed to the Prime Minister. A couple of weeks ago in this House he said if he received a plea for help from western farmers he would respond. Although he did not respond, while in the west last week, to the request by wheat producers and their organizations facing the worst financial crisis since the 1930s, now that he has been to the west and met with some farmers will he respond positively to their pleas for a deficiency payment for the 1987-88 crop year?

subsubtopic: WHEAT FARMERS-1987-88 CROP YEAR-REQUEST FOR DEFICIENCY PAYMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I met with western farmers throughout that area in a very good series of meetings last week. They were obviously concerned about the future because of the drop in commodity prices. They were very grateful for the $1 billion cash infusion which was the largest deficiency payment in the history of Canadian agriculture, designed by this Government. They were concerned about the future and so we resolved to work with them and their organizations, as well as the provinces, to alleviate as best we can any concern regarding next year.
Oral Questions

subtopic: REQUEST FOR INTRODUCTION OF NEW DEBT RESTRUCTURING INSTRUMENTS
REQUEST FOR INTRODUCTION OF NEW DEBT RESTRUCTURING INSTRUMENTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the farmers would be more pleased if they could get a commitment on the floor of this House today. Not only are they receiving the lowest prices since the 1930s in constant dollars, but are also suffering the worst devaluation in land values amounting to about $100,000 for the average economic sized farm.
Since the Prime Minister lifted the moratorium on FCC foreclosures will he make a commitment today to bring in new debt restructuring instruments to assist farmers facing foreclosure? Men and women who have worked for years and years and years now face the loss of their farms because no proper debt restructuring instruments were put in place by the Government to cope with this crisis.

subtopic: REQUEST FOR INTRODUCTION OF NEW DEBT RESTRUCTURING INSTRUMENTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the point raised by my hon. friend I find especially troubling. The thought that anyone who has worked the land with his family should, for whatever reason, lose that land or his right to it is something I find very troubling. I have examined with my colleagues, and will be examining with the provinces, further instruments whereby we can be helpful in that regard. I met specifically with a farmer and his son in Lethbridge, and then other farmers and their families outside Saskatoon, where this particular matter was discussed. I shall be working very closely with them in that regard.
I should tell my hon. friend, because I know he will be happy to hear it, that the farmers, while concerned about next year, are very grateful to this Parliament for the fact that aid to western agriculture, since this Government was sworn in, has increased by 350 per cent. They asked that their gratitude be conveyed to all Members.

Mr. Speaker, my question is directed to the Prime Minister. Having come back from western Canada after talking to some of our farmers I hope he now feels more personally the crisis that exists in western Canada. Whether he went to Alberta, Saskatchewan or Manitoba, surely the question that came up and again and again was what sort of long-term solutions is the Government working toward. Can the Prime Minister tell us what sort of long-term solutions the Government is prepared to offer to ensure that dozens of farm families will not go bankrupt? What long-term solutions is the Government thinking of and is prepared to offer?

Mr. Speaker, not only did the farmers raise the question of longterm solutions, they know full well there is no quick fix to the problems inflicted on western agriculture. They know no one in this House is responsible for the decline in commodity prices. They know full well that over the longer haul the answer is not greater and greater deficiency payments. They have increased their productivity and they do not want hand-outs. They want

May 11, 1987
Oral Questions
to be treated with dignity and respect and that is exactly what we are trying to do.
They also know, and discussed this very clearly with me, the work begun by this Government which for the first time raised agriculture at the level of the industrialized countries' summit in Tokyo last year.
A follow-up meeting is taking place right now at the OECD where the Minister of Finance and the Minister of International Trade are specifically dealing with international agricultural subsidies. That will be followed by a meeting convened in Canada of the Cairns group. That will be followed by meetings that the Secretary of State for External Affairs and I shall have with farm leaders before we take to the Venice Summit this very debilitating issue of the trade war and agricultural subsidies between the U.S. and the ECM. This is killing our western farmers. They do not deserve this kind of treatment and the Government is resolved with them to solve this longterm problem in the economy.

Mr. Speaker, western Canadian farmers recognize that the problem is the trade war between the U.S. and the ECM. They also recognize it will take a few years before that is resolved. They recognize as well, as one farmer is quoted as saying, that all the Government has come up with is short-term band-aid solutions. What they want to know is what thinking, if any, the Government is putting into finding a solution to keep them going and prevent thousands of farm families from going under until an international agreement is reached. Neither the Prime Minister nor his Government has given us any indication that some longterm thinking is being done. Is he prepared to make some definite announcements to Canadian farmers in the very near future if not today?

Mr. Speaker, my hon. friend is now asking quite a different question. The first question dealt with the long-term problem and I think we have attempted to deal with that. He is now turning his question to the problem of tomorrow as it affects the ordinary farmer in Saskatchewan. That, too, is absolutely vital.
What have we done? We brought about a reduction in interest rates of four percentage points, each of which saves farmers about $150 million in payments to financial institutions. We helped them reduce input costs. We increased direct support. We arranged for a degree of diversification. We brought about the largest single deficiency payment in the history of Canada.
We shall work with the farmers to make sure that they get through this critical period. As I said in western Canada, and I will tell my hon. friend again, with this Government, when western farmers cry out for support, there is someone here to answer them.

subtopic: EFFECT OF UNITED STATES FARM BILL
EFFECT OF UNITED STATES FARM BILL
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to follow up on the answers of the Prime Minister. He said the Government is taking all measures possible to deal with the immediate crisis in the West and the international trade problems.
The U.S. Government in the last two weeks has substantially expanded the U.S. Farm Bill to provide export subsidies to markets traditionally supplied by Canada. The U.S. is proposing further changes which would cause a further drop in prices. If the Government is interested in doing something for the western farmer is it prepared to take immediate action to forestall those actions which will have an even more damaging effect in the next six months on the farm economy of western Canada?
Right Hon. Joe Clark (Secretary of State for External
Affairs): Mr. Speaker, the Hon. Member's question was whether the Government has intervened with the United States administration with regard to various actions it is taking which are harmful to the interests of Canadian agriculture. The answer is that it certainly has and will continue to do so.
A discussion on precisely that matter occupied a large portion of the lunch convened by the Prime Minister for the President at 24 Sussex Drive in which the Prime Minister made clear, in no uncertain terms, Canada's grave concerns about the implications for Canadian production, and indeed for world trade in agriculture, of the U.S. Farm Bill. I will be carrying that message to San Francisco later this week when I meet with Secretary Shultz again.

Mr. Speaker, my supplementary question is directed to the Secretary of State for External Affairs. He just said that the matter was raised at a luncheon with the President. A week after that luncheon the President of the United States authorized his own administration to expand substantially farm exports in order to challenge Canadian traditional markets in both the Middle East and the Soviet Union. It must have been a hell of a luncheon discussion to get that result.
The point is that the Americans are continuing to move into those markets using their subsidy programs. What further action will we take to stop that kind of invasion of those markets and that use of the Farm Bill?
Has Canada responded to the proposal which was put forward by GATT several months ago for us to put our agricultural negotiating position on the table so that we know clearly what initiatives and priorities we have in agriculture? Are we going to do something deliberate to stop the United States taking that action? Have we put our proposals in front of GATT?
May 11, 1987

speakeroldname: Right Hon. Joe Clark (Secretary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, you know my natural modesty. I hesitate to suggest to the Hon. Member that he read the speech I gave to the Canada Grains Council in his own city about a month ago in which I set out quite precisely the five principles which Canada has advanced into the OECD and GATT which, if agreed to by other partners involved in international trade in agriculture, could begin much more quickly than in 10 years' time some movement away from the cycle of subsidy which we are now facing.
We intend to press this issue and the interests of Canadian farmers in international negotiations at every opportunity. We have been doing that and intend to continue to do that.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: I would like to advise the House that there will be a question and a supplementary question from the Hon. Member for Churchill followed by a single question from the Hon. Member for Drummond. That will close off Question Period.

Mr. Speaker, during the First Ministers' Conference last year the Prime Minister promised that there would be a full study of the impact of government policies on women. Has the Government undertaken a study to learn what the impact of the Government's free trade position is on women?

speakerposition: Minister responsible for the Status of Women; Minister of State (Privatization)
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the way in which the Government is approaching trade will result in the future of jobs and opportunity in Canada being very positive for women. Women do best in an atmosphere of growth, competition, and productivity. That is where women get real economic opportunities.
Allow me to point out that poor countries do not have a good record with regard to women. We want to ensure that there is prosperity, competition, and productivity in this country.

Mr. Speaker, I am sure the women of Canada appreciate the rhetoric, but I think they want to know whether the Government is going to live up to its promise to have a full impact study of its economic policy on free trade and how it affects women. Will that be made public?

speakerposition: Minister responsible for the Status of Women; Minister of State (Privatization)
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, no Government has done a better job for women than has this Government. There are 427,000 more women working today than there were on the day of the election.

Hear, hear!

speakerposition: Minister responsible for the Status of Women; Minister of State (Privatization)
speechtext: That is because we are looking forward and not to the past. We have employment equity, job training, trade which will expand job opportunities, more women working fulltime, and tax reform coming. All these things will work for the benefit of women in this country.

My question is for the Minister of Regional Industrial Expansion and deals with the textile industry. Last Friday night, one of our companies, Dominion Textiles, which manages its production in a very modern way, won the Regional Industrial Olympiad. Could the Minister guarantee the House that the textile policy will be followed, to allow the industry to continue and prosper in Canada.

speakeroldname: Hon. Michel Cote (Minister of Regional Industrial Expansion):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like, first of all, to congratulate that company on behalf of the Canadian Government.
Secondly, you may recall that the textile policy has been in effect since July 30th, 1986 and that its main objectives are to limit imports and to allow for a better control. According to information received from industry representatives, the industry is very pleased with the Government's policy which has led to a consolidation of employment and a streamlining of operations.

The House resumed consideration of the motion of Mr. Mulroney:
That this House endorses the Meech Lake statement of principles approved by all First Ministers, April 30, 1987 as a basis for Quebec's participation as a full partner in the Canadian Constitution, and as a basis for the establishment, in a spirit of equality and fairness, of a process for considering further constitutional reforms.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext:
When the House rose at one o'clock p.m. the Hon. Minister of Justice (Mr. Hnatyshyn) had completed his speech. I will now recognize Hon. Members who wish to question the Hon. Minister of Justice or comment on his speech. If there are none, we will resume debate.

May 11, 1987
The Constitution

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Liberal Party
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I would like to direct my question to the Minister of Justice (Mr. Elnatyshyn). With officials of his Department, he is preparing the final legal text of constitutional changes agreed upon at the Meech Lake meeting. Could the Minister tell the House when this text will be ready? Could he guarantee the House that we will have an opportunity to debate the proposed resolution before it is submitted for approval to the provincial Premiers?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my Department has been working, on an urgent priority basis, on the wording which will be submitted to the First Ministers. As the Hon. Member will appreciate, the process will involve discussions among the participants and those First Ministers who must take that step in a constitutional sense to ensure that the wording is satisfactory for First Ministers to take to their respective legislatures. We are working on it on a very urgent basis.
Bilateral discussions are, of course, taking place. We are quite prepared, through participation in this debate, to hear points of view. It is very helpful to hear comments of all Members of Parliament.
With regard to the manner in which this whole proposition can be dealt with, I think that would be best left to discussions between the House Leaders to find the most appropriate methods of dealing with the matter.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Liberal Party
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, my question really deals with the legal text. Will the Minister give his undertaking today that he will table in the House the legal text before-and I emphasize "before"-it is brought to the Premiers for their approval so that we can discuss the legal text in this House?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I do not quite understand what the Hon. Member is suggesting. The Hon. Member may not have meant that we should somehow ignore the First Ministers with regard to discussions about the text, but that would be the result of his proposal.
I believe there will be opportunities for Hon. Members to study the legal text at the appropriate time. I do not want to suggest for a moment that we are going to ignore the First Ministers. The matter will be discussed with them to ensure that we have something with which we can move, on the same basis as we arrived at the consensus which the Hon. Member, his Leader, and his Party have indicated in this debate that they support absolutely.

Mr. Speaker, the Minister and his Government have made provision for this House to debate for days, weeks, and perhaps even months, the death penalty. We are debating this proposal for one day. Would the Minister of Justice (Mr. Hnatyshyn) care to comment on the strange sense of priority which allows the Government to find a lot of time for the death penalty debate and only one day for debate on this very important measure?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I do not know if I can give a satisfactory answer to the Hon. Member. I think the position on the capital punishment debate is that Members on the government side are prepared to have this matter go to a vote right now and that the opposition Members want to talk on this for quite a long time. I am not disputing the right of the Hon. Members to have-

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Liberal Party
speechtext: It is supposed to be a free vote.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
1 am just giving my view of life in the House of Commons and why, when Members ask me a question, they sometimes do not mean what they purport to say. I am trying to put this into perspective.
I can tell the Hon. Member, as I said in my remarks, that I think it is important. I believe he would agree with me because he is a man of principle who stands up regardless of pressures, some that are even brought on him by colleagues in his own caucus. He would understand that this is a matter of very important leadership. It has been in the public domain and I do not understand why we cannot have a vote at the end of the day showing that we all support it, because everyone has stated they are in favour of it. It is important to us that the principle is decided.
The Hon. Member knows that the opposition Parties have many opportunities to raise this issue in whatever context they want. Allotted opposition days are always available to them. I believe, in terms of the time that should be made available for this very historic occasion, his House leader should meet with the Government House Leader; I am sure they can come to an understanding about what is appropriate in dealing with these matters.
Personally, I believe the principle is important, one on which we should have a vote to show the unanimity with which we accept Quebec in the Constitution, and the prospect of a continuing role for other provinces in western Canada and Atlantic Canada to bring matters onto the agenda, as well as the two central provinces. I believe this is a wonderful day in Canadian history, and I am glad the Hon. Member's Party is supporting this Agreement.

Mr. Speaker, I want to ask the Minister of Justice (Mr. Hnatyshyn) a question with respect to an important element of this Accord that has not yet received a great deal of attention, the element with respect to the naming of appointees to the Supreme Court of Canada.
The Supreme Court of Canada is one of the most important institutions in our land now and, of course, has increasing importance in Canada in view of its powers the Charter of Rights and to interpret the provisions of the Constitution itself.
Will the Minister explain why the Government gave away the power of the Prime Minister of Canada (Mr. Mulroney) to choose the best possible man or woman from the provinces or the regions to sit on that court? We strongly support consultation with the provinces before Supreme Court of
May 11, 1987

Canada judges are named, but what will happen in the event that the nominees of the province or a particular region are unacceptable to the Government, yet the particular province insists it wants to maintain that list? How will this deadlock between the provinces and the federal Government be broken?
Finally, if the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) wants to appoint a particular outstanding man or woman from one of the provinces but that person is not even on the list that has been submitted by the province, the federal Government's hands are tied.
Why has the Government accepted a proposal which could very seriously weaken the Supreme Court of Canada?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I find that to be an incredible proposition on the part of the New Democratic Party. 1 must ask the Hon. Member again, as I do on so many occasions, if his question reflects the position of his Leader and Party. If he is speaking as an individual Member, I understand, but if the New Democratic Party is suggesting that Premier Pawley should have no role in terms of the appointments of a Supreme Court judge, 1 do not accept that proposition.
I suggest that in this country the Government has at least demonstrated the ability to work in a co-operative federalism with a view to having real consultation. I say to the Hon. Member that naturally it is a decision to be made by the federal Government in the final analysis, but to be made on the basis of names put forward. There will be a real sense of participation, partnership, and discussion in the process of appointing judges to the Supreme Court of Canada.
I know the Hon. Member believes that it is important to ensure that all regions of Canada are dealt with equitably. Both of us are from western Canada and he would want to make sure that western Canadian premiers and Governments duly elected by western Canadians can send a strong signal as to the composition of the court and its western representatives.
I do not look at this in a negative sense, but as a positive way in which we can develop and encourage co-operative federalism. I do not anticipate a deadlock situation, quite the contrary.

Mr. Speaker, after the bafflegab of the Minister, perhaps he could answer the very specific question. What happens if Grant Devine or Bill Vander Zalm submit to the Prime Minister of Canada names of people who are clearly not acceptable to sit on the Supreme Court of Canada, the federal Government returns those names to the Premier but the Premier insists on putting those names forward? What mechanism will there be to break a deadlock between the federal and provincial Governments in the naming of the judges to the highest court of the land? How will that be done?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is a hypothetical situation. In this case, as in so many cases, my own experience has demonstrated that, by and large, the whole appointment process is one in which it is possible to have sane and legitimate discussions with provincial Premiers and Governments.
The Constitution
I do not think it is appropriate to assume that these matters of national interest begin with the lowest common denominator. I do not believe that is the Canadian way. It is inconceivable to me that the federal Government and the western premiers could not find some consensus with respect to the name of an appointee to represent western Canada. 1 suggest that it has not happened and will not happen. I believe we will be able to find support for a representative person who has the prime criterion of competence with respect to the Supreme Court of Canada.
I hope that we do not consider this constitutional discussion on a negative basis because constitutional building involves a very substantial element of understanding and trust. Our present Constitution contains many concepts that are not precisely defined, but they have not impeded us from having an outstanding country and one in which we can carry on, to the benefit of Canadians. I simply say to the Hon. Member that that is the attitude I take in this process. I hope the Hon. Member will agree.

Mr. Speaker, I want to return to the important subject raised by my colleague concerning the procedure that will be followed. We were asking whether we could debate the resolution before it is formally approved by the 11 First Ministers. The Minister of Justice (Mr. Hnatyshyn) suggested in his answer that somehow this would not be possible because the resolution that would come here will be drafted in consultation with the 11 First Ministers. Surely there is no inconsistency. Once the formal approval is applied to that resolution, it is very difficult for the Government to seriously consider practical suggestions that might be made by our Party or the New Democratic Party.
I hope there will be consultation in the preparation of the final resolution, but will the Minister of Justice undertake that however the final resolution is prepared, before it goes to the level of First Ministers' approval there will be good faith by the Government to present that resolution to us in the Chamber to allow the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Turner), our Members, and Members of the New Democratic Party to make the kinds of suggestions that were given in 1981 when the Opposition participated fully in the constitutional proposals? Will we have a similar opportunity to make constructive suggestions for consideration by the Government before the First Ministers meet and put on the seal of approval on the final package?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, first, I think we should remember that constitutional amendment was created by the 1982 enactment and proclamation. It was a Government, of which the Hon. Member was a distinguished Member, that brought us to the reality that in order to bring about a Constitution, we must have the assent of First Ministers; in certain cases a percentage of the provincial Legislature; ana in some cases we must have a unanimous proposition. Right now we have the prospect of a unanimous approach by all Premiers representing all political Parties of our country and the federal Government. I simply say that we have to take these matters in logical step.

May 11, 1987
The Constitution
The Hon. Member's House Leader can discuss with the Government House Leader and the House Leader for the New Democratic Party the appropriate way to deal with this matter. We must have a starting point. Unless we can come to some arrangement with respect to the wording with the First Ministers, there is nothing very useful for us to discuss. We have to be able to get that agreement.
I am saying to the Hon. Member that we have a proposition which will allow Hon. Members to declare themselves. It is not a question of keeping it from the House. The House will have a chance to declare itself. We have taken the first step to talk on this occasion on a statement of principle, to hear from Hon. Members, particularly from opposition Members, as to where they stand on the issues and to have their suggestions as to what should be included or not included. We are listening and we are going to try to do the very best job we can. I think our record in this area is pretty good. We have had unanimity and I hope we will continue to have the support of the Hon. Member's Party.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: I would like to advise Hon. Members that the time for questions and comments has expired. 1 am in the hands of the House. Is there agreement to extend?
Agreed.
No.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: Debate.

Over the years, Mr. Speaker, this House has certainly been the scene of major debates which, in more ways than one, have highlighted the history of our country. The one we are launching today is one more such debate, for the main concept underlying the Meech Lake constitutional agreement reflects the very heart of the country which Canadian men and women choose to build every day. As the Right Hon. the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Turner) said in the House of Commons last May 1 after the Meech Lake agreement was announced, and I quote:
It is a happy day for Canada and for Quebec, particularly for all those who
believed that our country would remain united by respecting the diversity of its
regions and the equality of its citizens.
At the outset of my remarks I want to tell the House that I intend to support the general thrust of the Meech Lake agreement as endorsed by the 10 Provincial Premiers of Canada. I would also advise the House that, in accordance with the position set forth by the Leader of the Opposition, I will vote in favour of the motion submitted for the consideration of the House by the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney).
Mr. Speaker, 1 would also add that, after consulting most of my colleagues from Quebec and the other provinces, we are looking at a process which, although it may contain certain difficulties, constitutes an orientation which enables us today
to support the Meech Lake constitutional evolution. Need I recall that one of the reasons which prompted me to return to active political life, this time at the federal level, was to fight to find a way to make the adjustments required so that Quebec would at last sign the 1982 constitutional agreement? Despite my profound Quebec and francophone roots, and despite the diverging views we might entertain on some of the aspects of the Meech Lake agreement, I trust that nobody will question my dedication to fight for Canadian unity.
When I was a Cabinet Member in the Government of the Province of Quebec, my provincial Liberal colleagues and I fought against the independence movement then advocated by Pierre Bourgault, Gilles Gregoire and, finally, Rene Levesque.
I defended Canadian unity in the Quebec National Assembly, in the universities, and in discussions at CEGEPs, at a time when even families were divided on the question of whether Quebec should be part of Canada.
I remember how shattered many Quebecers were, and with them the Bourassa Government's young Cabinet, when they heard our colleague, Pierre Laporte, had been killed. Pierre Laporte, a great Quebecer and a nationalist, lost his life in circumstances that are now history, in the defence of Canadian unity. I remember the tense social climate in the province at the time of the constitutional conference in Victoria, only a few months after Mr. Laporte's murder. When people ask why the Bourassa Government at the time was reluctant to support the Victoria Charter, my answer is this: Remember the political and social climate in Quebec after the October Crisis in 1970.
It would have been easy for me and for so many people of my generation to give in to popular pressure and succumb to the mass movement like so many young Quebecers who were entranced with the idea of political sovereignty for Quebec. Like so many colleagues in the Quebec Liberal Party and the federal Liberal Party, however, I did not give in to those pressures because I believed that the independence option was an illusion and that the greater interests of francophones in Quebec and elsewhere in Canada would be far better served within Canada, within a "renewed" Canada, than by an independence formula that, sooner or later, would have isolated Quebec, both economically and culturally, linguistically and socially. The hopes of Canadian federalists who stood up for national unity in Quebec rested on a "renewed Canada". A new federalism that would meet Quebec's aspirations, that was the message members of the Trudeau Government brought to Quebec in 1980.
That was the concept we defended during the referendum, and because the majority of Quebecers believed in the concept of an evolving federation, they voted no in the referendum. And I say to my anglophone colleagues on both sides of the
May 11, 1987

House that they should never forget this fact, because it is fundamental to the debate we have begun today.
The then Prime Minister and the provincial Premiers who took part in the referendum debate clearly indicated their desire to do everything they could to find a balance that would be acceptable to Quebecers within the Canadian federation, in recognition of the fact that because of its language, its civil code, its history and its traditions, Quebec had a distinct identity within the Canadian federation.
Thanks to the 1982 Constitutional Accord, this country was able to achieve several objectives which I supported at the time and still do. The entrenchment of a Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms in the Canadian Constitution and the patriation of the Constitution to make Canada a fully sovereign state, capable of changing the basic laws of our country right here, without having to go to a foreign parliament-these were major, positive steps.
I have always thought, and I still do, that although the 1982 Constitutional Accord did not meet the legitimate aspirations of Quebecers who support national unity, it was because at the negotiating table, a separatist Quebec government was seeking formulas that would support its concept of independence, not the unity or enhanced unity of this country.
The 1982 Constitutional Accord was an unfinished symphony, and to finish it, it was necessary to approach the Quebec question in such a way that the parties concerned would accept the premise that no solution would be possible without recognition of Quebec's distinct identity within the Canadian federation. Quebec would also need the assurance that the rules of the constitutional game would not be changed with respect to the fundamental tenets of the federation, without the consent of the province of Quebec.
Therefore, in addition to the recognition of the distinct character of Quebec, the new constitutional balance was to provide security to Quebec at two different levels; first, at the level of immigration and second, at the level of the amending formula. The Meech Lake Accord positively answers the immigration issue. 1 do not intend to deal further with this matter on which there seems to be a general consensus. Moreoever, the resolution that was passed by the Liberal Party of Canada at its convention in November, 1986, stated somewhat the same idea which is to entrench in the Canadian Constitution the Cullen-Couture agreement.
As for the amending formula, I readily admit that I would much rather have the Victoria formula than that contained in the Meech Lake Accord. The Leader of the Official Opposition stated this morning some reservations which I share not only with regard to the amending formula but also about the meaning of some words appearing in the Meech Lake Accord. The intent of the legislator should be clearly indicated. Otherwise, the problems which were supposed to be solved could be compounded in the future. For example, there are some sincere and honest concerns about the capacity of the
The Constitution
Government of Canada as a result of the Meech Lake Accord to intervene in regional economic development.
I do not think that we can brush aside these concerns simply because they are voiced by people from Atlantic Canada, Manitoba or Quebec. In my opinion, as we deal with this problem, we must bear in mind that the wording should be precise enough so that the text of the Constitution does not say things that are not intended and does not cause unnecessary division. I shall take spending power as an example.
I could go into a fiery plea against the limitation of spending power and argue that Quebec should never have accepted this text, since for the first time in the history of our country, it shall be written in the Canadian Constitution that the Federal Government has the right to intervene in matters of exclusive provincial jurisdiction. But I do not believe that such is the intent, as some would see it, since the argument of those who are against the limitation of spending power is the exact opposite.
I therefore submit that it should be possible to give a precise wording to what was the intent of the Prime Minister and the Premiers who met at Meech Lake. In my view, it is simply a question of coming to an understanding which will avoid unnecessary disputes in the future.
Coming back to the amending formula, I can say that given the circumstances and taking it for granted that what is essential has been preserved, since Quebec, as the other provinces of Canada, shall have a right of veto with regard to those institutions which are fundamental to the Canadian federation, I feel that the compromise which has been reached is essentially adequate and reasonable and that it deserves to be supported.
