May 11, 1987
The Constitution

First, Mr. Speaker, 1 would like to commend the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) and the 10 Premiers for the unanimous agreement reached at Meech Lake.
Mr. Speaker, thanks to the Meech Lake Accord, Quebec would be part of the Canadian family as far as the Constitution of Canada is concerned. And as the Prime Minister stated this morning, seven years ago Quebec said yes to Canada, and now it is time for Canada to say yes to Quebec.

We now have an agreement which is very important in bringing Quebec into this constitutional family of Canada. I believe Canadians outside of Quebec, through their various provincial Premiers, have shown a great openness to Quebec, particularly when they have talked about Quebec being a distinct and different society. They made a considerable move toward bringing Quebec into the Constitution. I now invite Quebec to show the same kind of leadership in trying to bring about solutions to some of the other constitutional problems that face other parts of the country, and I particularly invite Quebec and the other provinces to show the same kind of leadership in bringing our native Indian people into the Constitution of Canada.

Mr. Speaker, it is ironic in that perhaps the process of change to our Canadian Constitution started on November 15, 1976, with the election to Government of the Parti Quebecois and Premier Rene Levesque in Quebec. That election was followed by a referendum in Quebec three years and a half later, on May 20, 1980.

After that referendum, we had a debate in the House and across the country about patriating the Canadian Constitution. We went from that step to what is before us today in the Meech Lake Agreement.
The Constitution of Canada is the fundamental law of this country. It is the foundation on which all other laws are based. The Constitution does not belong to the Governments, to the politicians or to the bureaucrats. The Constitution belongs to the people of Canada.
Today I reaffirm my belief in federalism. It is federalism that makes this country work. In particular, I reaffirm my belief in a system of co-operative federalism, the only way in which a country as diverse as Canada can work at all.
There are two orders of Government in this country and there must continue to be two orders of Government. On the one hand, it is very important to have a strong and central federal Government and we need that strong and central federal Government to equalize things between the various regions and, as much as possible, between the various people of the country, whether they come from a wealthy part or a poorer part of Canada. On the other hand, in addition to a
strong and central federal Government, we need strong provincial Governments with their own jurisdictions because of the differing realities in each province and region. Those two orders of Government must be equal partners if Canada is to have a national dream and a national vision toward which we all must work.
I suppose I can say that federalism means both uniting the country and decentralizing it at the same time. To me, federalism means a compromise between a unitary system such as those that exist in Britain or in France on the one hand and independent, sovereign states on the other. Federalism is a compromise. Federalism is co-operation. I think it is very important that we see it in that way.
In addition to that, federalism is more than just co-operation between the federal Government and the provinces and the various other Governments. Federalism is about the two founding peoples who many years ago founded this great country, the English and the French. It is also about the prefounding people, the native people. There are many different Indian nations that were here a long time before our predecessors came from Europe and other parts of the world.
In addition to that, federalism is about the various cultures that exist in Canada. I suppose you can tell by my name, Mr. Speaker, that I come from neither an anglophone nor a francophone background but that I come from a third group of countries that is neither British nor French.
Our differences should unite us, they should not divide us. It should be the differences that make this country flourish. We all benefit from the fact that we are not one great, gigantic melting pot. In fact, one of the big differences between Canada and the United States is that the United States tends to be very much of a melting pot.
A person from my riding named Alex Kuziak was the first Canadian of Ukrainian ancestry to ever be appointed to a Cabinet anywhere in Canada. He was appointed to the Cabinet of Saskatchewan by Tommy Douglas back in 1948. In 1969, a year after I came to Parliament as a Member, we were debating the Official Languages Act. There was much uncertainty in parts of Canada. It was felt that perhaps too many rights were being given to French-speaking Canadians and it was wondered if there should be equality of languages and if Quebec was getting too much power. I recall Mr. Kuziak rising in a meeting held in Yorkton to say that the one reason there is more tolerance of minority languages, customs and cultures in Canada is the very fact that we do have two big language groups, the French and the English. Because of that, he said, we are also more tolerant of others. That is one of the things that makes this country different from the United States of America.
To begin with, Canada is in some ways very difficult to keep together. We defy geography and the natural north-south trading patterns. We also sit right next door to the most powerful nation in the world and we must protect our sovereignty, culture and economy. Those things make it very
May 11, 1987

difficult to begin with. That is why it is very important that all Canadians pull together to try to form national goals and objectives.
In the few minutes that remain I want to comment specifically on parts of the resolution before us. With regard to Quebec and a distinct society-

-I would like to say yes to the particular society of Quebec, to that distinct society. I have long said that Quebec is different and that the fact has to be recognized in the Constitution. I enthusiastically support this proposition of the 11 First Ministers.
I also want to mention, Mr. Speaker, that Quebec ... It is not only the fact that Quebec is unique and distinct, but also that it is the main cultural centre for all French-speaking Canadians.

I also want to say that even though I very deeply respect the Hon. Member for Saint-Henri-Westmount (Mr. Johnston), I think his point of view with respect to Quebec and a distinct society is a point of view of yesterday. It is an idea of yesterday. It is a vision of yesterday. I do not think that is the way Canadians want to go today.
I want to comment about the regrettable fact that our native people are not part of this constitutional Accord at Meech Lake. I know the Prime Minister has had conferences on this issue. I know he and several Premiers have supported enshrining more aboriginal rights in the Constitution. I support him. 1 would just say it is very unfortunate and regrettable that the people who were here before all of us are not part of the constitutional family when we seek to bring Quebec into the Constitution. I say very clearly that I am not proud of the Premier of my province, Mr. Devine, because he did not agree to the enshrinement of Indian self-government in the Constitution. I am not proud of Premier Don Getty of Alberta or Premier Vander Zalm of British Columbia for not agreeing to enshrine more Indian rights in the Constitution of Canada. We should be expressing our feelings to those three Premiers who were the main stumbling blocks to doing just that a few weeks ago. My understanding is that the other Premiers and the Prime Minister were ready to move but the three Premiers from the westernmost provinces said no, no, no, and I believe that is wrong.

Another aspect, Mr. Speaker, is immigration. I agree with the Meech Lake Agreement as far as the question of immigration is concerned. It enshrines in the Constitution more rights for Quebec in that field. The Government of Canada can also negociate with a province an immigration agreement.
The Constitution

Another point concerns the Senate. Under the Meech Lake Agreement there is talk about the provinces having more input on the appointment of Senators. There is a commitment to enshrine in the Constitution discussions on Senate reform. I believe that the Senate as it exists today should be abolished. It is nothing but a house of patronage.
Hear, hear!
I do not think there is any place in the 20th century for an unelected legislative body.
There was not in the 19th century either.

Not in the 19th century either. Our Party remains open to replacing the Senate with some other institution if it is abolished. I speak only for myself but I certainly remain very open to the possibility of having the Senate in some way reflect the regions in its representation. For example, there might be an equal number of Senators from each province. We have to make sure the Senate is elected.
Another point I am concerned about concerns spending power. This is something a number of us are concerned about. We believe we need to have on the one hand a strong federal Government that can implement national programs like medicare, unemployment insurance and family allowances, and on the other hand, we need to have enough flexibility so that the provinces can represent their own reality and recognize the diversity of this country. I am by no means a constitutional lawyer or expert, but I want to raise a concern about the drafting of the section which deals with spending power. It says that the provinces can undertake their own initiatives or programs with compatible national objectives. After hearing a number of commentaries I am not sure whether the word "compatible" is strong enough to protect the national interest. Perhaps instead of "compatible" we should be looking at "equivalent" provincial programs. There should be minimum standards that must be met. If not, there would be no compensation.
Coming from Saskatchewan I well remember the medicare fight when Woodrow Lloyd was the Premier and the big fight was over establishing medical care in 1962. I remember the tremendous opposition to medicare. The vested interests fought very hard against it. A little bit later on I remember the royal commission headed by Mr. Justice Emmett Hall on this question and the debate when Prime Minister Pearson was in office. Tommy Douglas was the Leader of this Party. John Diefenbaker was the Leader of the Conservative Party. I remember how close we came to not getting national medicare. I am really concerned that we do not enshrine in the Constitution wording which would be so interpreted by the courts as to make it impossible to get those kinds of national programs in the future.

If not, you run the danger of having a much better program in Ontario, which is wealthy, than in Newfoundland, which is poor. We could have a much better program in British Columbia or Alberta if the western economy picks up again than we have, for example, in New Brunswick or Prince Edward Island because they are much smaller and much poorer. I appeal to the Prime Minister to try to get an agreement to entrench wording which would protect the national interest.
I want to comment on the creation of new provinces. This is one part of the Agreement I do not agree with at all. I do not know why the rules should be different for the creation of new provinces in the Northwest Territories or Yukon than they were when Saskatchewan, Alberta and other provinces were created. In the past there was an agreement between the province concerned and the federal Government. The province came into the federation, and that was it. If the First Ministers are not willing to continue with that as a fall back, as my Leader said today, we certainly accept the existing amending formula where seven provinces representing 50 per cent of the population and the Parliament of Canada have to agree. In that way one or two provinces cannot veto Yukon becoming a province. I am not sure if Mr. Vander Zalm, for example, would agree to Yukon becoming a province. I think the existing amending formula would be much fairer for Yukon. I once again appeal to the Prime Minister and the Minister of Justice (Mr. Hnatyshyn) to look very seriously at that idea.
I am also concerned about the unanimity rule as it concerns national institutions, and I am particularly concerned when it comes to the Senate. I recognize the special problems of Quebec with respect to protecting the French language and culture. However, I am concerned about whether or not we have created a bit of a strait-jacket here for Senate reform. Under the present rules, Saskatchewan, British Columbia and Alberta get six Senators, but New Brunswick and Nova Scotia get 10 apiece. We are now going to have a system where the Premiers recommend potential Senators and the federal Government must pick someone from the list acceptable to it. I am not sure whether Richard Hatfield or another Premier of New Brunswick, or the Premier of Nova Scotia, want to give up that power and that number of Senators. I am just not sure those Premiers would be more interested in doing that now than they were three or four weeks ago. I am not sure whether David Peterson of Ontario would like to give up this new-found power of recommending 20 or 24 people as Senators. If that does not happen there will be great discrimination because Saskatchewan and British Columbia have only six Senators each while Ontario and Quebec have 20 or 24 apiece. That is a major problem.
I know other Members would like to say a few words before six o'clock. I will, therefore, conclude by saying that we have,
in general, a good agreement in principle. I am concerned about a number of the details, particularly the spending power. I am concerned about the amending formula as it pertains to the creation of new provinces. I am very concerned that the Indian people did not have more rights enshrined in the Constitution. I appeal to the Premier of my province, the Premiers of the other provinces, and the Prime Minister of Canada to do whatever they can to make this a better deal for the country.
I agree that we have a tremendous future and a great country. When we fully patriate the Constitution of Canada we can start working on some of the very serious economic problems, patriate the economy of Canada, and create an economy within which we can wipe out poverty for every Canadian.

Mr. Speaker, my hon. colleague, the Member for Yorkton-Melville (Mr. Nystrom), referred to the position taken by our friend from Saint-Henri-Westmount. He said that he believed that position was outdated in 1987. I agree with that statement. As a neighbour of my good friend from Saint-Henri-Westmount I must say that in my opinion he has exaggerated the possible negative interpretations of the Accord. In any case, I think he was premature in his remarks.
When the Liberal Party passed its resolution in November of 1986 it said that a preamble should be added to the Constitution of Canada to recognize the linguistic duality of Canada and the distinctive character of Quebec as the principal but not exclusive source of the French language and culture of Canada. It seems to me that that is not too far from what we have in the Accord. As we have all said, we will want to see the final wording.
I know my friend has a deep interest in the rights of minorities and he has already referred to native people. Section (1) of the Accord states that:
The Constitution of Canada shall be interpreted in a manner consistent with a) the recognition that the existence of French-speaking Canada, centred in but not limited to Quebec, and English-speaking Canada, concentrated outside Quebec but also present in Quebec, constitutes a fundamental characteristic of Canada;
Section (2) says:
Parliament and the provincial legislatures-are committed to preserving the
fundamental characteristics of Canada-
Would the Hon. Member not agree with me that that provides adequate protection to the linguistic minorities of the country? It appears to me that it does, and I am one who voted against the agreement in 1982. What is the Hon. Member's opinion on that?

Mr. Speaker, I think there is adequate protection for the linguistic minorities. There is reference in the constitutional agreement In the first section with regard to the distinct society, "the recognition that the existence of French-speaking Canada, centred in but not limited to Quebec, and English-speaking Canada, concentrated outside Quebec but also present in Quebec". It also refers to the role

of the National Assembly in Quebec in terms of achieving this distinctiveness. It refers, in addition, to legislatures outside of Quebec and the Parliament of Canada.
I would also remind my friend, the Hon. Member for Notre-Dame-de-Grace-Lachine East (Mr. Allmand) of Section 23 of the Canada Act which talks about minority languages and education rights within those minority languages. It says that all provinces must provide education in the minority language where numbers warrant. Therefore, I think we are covered pretty well in terms of protecting minority language rights.
As more of an opinion than a fact I would say that one way of protecting the French language from coast-to-coast is to ensure that there is very strong protection of it in Quebec. The French language is a minority language in this country and an even smaller minority in North America. We can protect the French language across Canada by protecting it very solidly in Quebec, ensuring that it is not eroded there. If it is solidly protected there, that can help it flourish right across the country.
The English language is very well protected because it is the most important language in the world today. It is the majority language in North America as it is in this country. One way to protect minority rights is to ensure that we have two secure linguistic bases. If people do not feel insecure about that, both can flourish on each other's turf, so to speak.

Mr. Speaker, Canada is a country of tolerance which is in the process of becoming united again with full respect for its differences.
Mr. Speaker, in the early 1980s I joined the team of the present Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) because 1 believed he could manage to create a new climate of harmony in Canada and make Canadians regain their aspirations for genuine federalism. I believed he would be able to put an end to the sterile squabbles among the various regions of the country.

I believe that such a change could create a new relationship between Canadians, a more creative, tolerant and generous relationship between Canadians.

Finally I believed that the new climate might bring us to the day when Quebec would regain its place within Canada's constitutional forums. All those who, like myself, responded to the Prime Minister's appeal also believed in this change. Men and women in Quebec put their faith in us because they were convinced we would succeed in making this great change. This faith in the possibility of changing things has never been a blind faith. The man who is now Prime Minister then made a firm commitment to Quebec.
As he said in August 1984, all Quebecers love Quebec and are proud of Canada, but they also love Canada and are proud of Quebec. Their heart is big enough for both allegiances. He said that Canada offers plenty of room for the affirmation of all identities, the respect for all aspirations, and the quest for all ideals.
To heal the wounds of 1982, for wounds had indeed been inflicted to Quebec, he had solemnly pledged to do everything possible to convince the National Assembly to accept the new Constitution with honour and enthusiasm. Well, on April 30, something extraordinary happened, because his commitment to Quebec was not restricted to a single election campaign, or a vague promise to win over part of the nationalist electorate. This commitment is part of his vision of Canada and Canadians based on fairness, equity and generosity.
The Prime Minister has always appealed to the noblest and highest values held by Canadian men and women to defend the rights of minorities, linguistic and otherwise, and to defend the people and the regions of our country. He has always believed that it is through respect for our differences that we shall find new strength to stay together.
It is with enthusiasm that I came to Ottawa to defend the interests, first of Quebec, and also of the rest of Canada, but I came also because our new Prime Minister had promised us to do everything to restore Quebec to its rightful place within Confederation.
Today, Mr. Speaker, this major task is well on its way towards accomplishment.

The Prime Minister of Canada, the Premier of Quebec, along with the other Premiers have agreed in principle, which will permit the Province of Quebec to join the constitutional family and permit Quebecers to be true Canadians.

This is indeed important: To be a true French Canadian, it is necessary, in my opinion, for me to be a Canadian.

I am also proud of what has been accomplished at Meech Lake. It is not to be perceived as being a gesture of favour to Quebec, because it was a gesture of favour to all provinces.
They have also agreed to include in the Constitution an aspect of utmost importance to our national identity.

The Constitutional Act of 1982 was to a great extent a description of the characteristics which make Canada unique. Yet, there was no mention anywhere in the Constitution of Quebec's distinct society or the existence in Canada of francophone and anglophone communities.
In the absence of these two basic realities, how was our commitment to linguistic minority rights to be interpreted? How else were we to show respect for Quebecers' desire to affirm themselves proudly as full partners in our national design, as partners equal but different through their history and institutions? I suggest that the Prime Minister was well aware that there was an important gap to be filled, and he appealed to the open mind and generosity of his counterparts to ensure a successful conclusion to the Meech Lake exercise. This was a necessary gamble, because solving this problem did not depend entirely on the Government of Canada, but also on the Governments of Quebec and the other provinces.
All the provinces, therefore, had to participate in the development of a new Constitutional consensus which would take into account the legitimate aspirations of Quebecers, but also the basic interests of all other Canadians. The Prime Minister felt also that, to be fair, any agreement would have to take place within the context of a true federalism. The support of all Governments was necessary, the opinion of each had to be taken into account. The country had suffered enough from partisan agreements, behind-the-scene maneuvers, deals negotiated with no real consensus.

All Premiers were aware of the damages that would result from another failure. No one placed himself into an irrevocable position. Quebec was also just and generous. When it asked that its distinct character be recognized, it did not do so with a desire for isolation. It could have, but it did not. On the contrary, Quebec insisted that its specificity be recognized for a broader reality: one of existence of a francophone Canada, concentrated and not limited to Quebec, and one of an anglophone Canada, concentrated in the rest of the country but present in Quebec.

That is the essence of the agreement, is it not? The recognition of the existence of French-speaking Canada centred in but not limited to Quebec, and that of English-speaking Canada concentrated in the rest of the country but also highly present in Quebec.
Therefore, the First Ministers agreed to enshrine this fundamental characteristic of the federation into the Constitution. That simple recognition has already allowed Quebecers to stand proud, and that is what we achieved on the evening of April 30, to the surprise of everyone.

However, the Lake Meech Agreement is more than that. The First Ministers recognized the importance of our two main language communities for our national identity. It is perhaps because they sensed the delicate balance that they committed themselves to protect that reality.
In the future, the Constitution shall necessarily be interpreted with due regard for the existence of our two linguistic communities and for the fact that Quebec constitutes a distinct society. This is what is fundamental and this is what is important to us.
This agreement, Mr. Speaker, is therefore a victory for all members of official language minorities in Canada. It grants recognition to the two main communities and to their existence in every region of the country, and this is in tune with the

I am proud to see, Mr. Speaker, that our Prime Minister and our Premiers have chosen first and foremost to be statesmen rather than power hungry petty politicians: this is fundamental. So I say today that I am proud of you, Brian Mulroney, as a Quebecer, which you are, but also as a Canadian, which you are as well for all of us: I am very proud of you.
